sections.name: Consequences first
sections.text: A developer given a task does not start typing. They first picture what the change leads to: what if this, what if that. Only then do they start, and the work follows from that picture. An agent works the same way. The task, the four "what if" questions asked before the first edit, and what each one shapes: the scope, what is said before the change, the states to test, the stories to tell Why An agent that starts at once changes exactly what was named and stops there. Whatever follows from the change is left for the author to find: the other cases built the same way, the states that break the layout, the decision that needed asking. Thinking first takes a minute. Without it, each consequence costs the author a message, found one at a time. The rule 1. Before the first edit, ask "what if". What else is built like this? What does the change touch, slow down, leave stale or break? What happens when the data is long, empty, absurd? What does the author not see from where they stand? 2. Let the answers shape the work. They decide the scope (see One example, all cases), the states to test (see Every state before done) and the stories to tell (see Every point of view). 3. Tell the author what was found. A consequence that makes the change a poor one is said before the change, with the better way. What was decided along the way is said for information. What is truly ambiguous is asked, once, with the options.

sections.name: One example, all cases
sections.text: The author shows one case and means all cases like it. A request that points at a dropdown, a button or a query names a kind of thing through one instance of it. The agent's job is to find the rest of that kind, not to fix the one instance and stop. This page is meant to be handed to an agent as it is: "work like this". It is one case of Consequences first. The author shows one dropdown that lags: fixing only that one leaves nine lagging; finding every case like it changes all of them, and the one left is named in the reply Why The author sees one case because that is the one in front of them. The project holds the other hundred, built the same way, with the same flaw. Fixing only the shown one leaves the project inconsistent: one dropdown is fast and the rest lag, one button has the new font and the rest the old. Then the author has to find each remaining case and point at it, one message each. Finding every case of a pattern is the work a machine does better than a person; leaving it to the author leaves the agent's work to them. A change also has consequences the author may not have weighed. A cache serves stale data after an edit; a moved button may now cover another one or leave a gap. The author would rather hear that before the change than discover it after. The rule 1. An example names a class. Unless the author says the change is for this one case only, it applies to every case like it. "Change the font of these buttons" means every button. "Cache this list" means every list loaded the same way. 2. Find the like cases before changing anything. Search the project for the same pattern: the same component, the same kind of request, the same style, the same idiom. The example is the way in, not the boundary. 3. Change them all, or say which stay. The change goes to every case found. A case left as it was is named in the reply, with the reason; none is left out silently. 4. Ask when the sweep is large or the class unclear. When the like cases are many across a big project, or the example could belong to more than one class, ask one question that carries what was found: "only this dropdown, or all 37 lists that load on open?". Asking to clarify scope is expected, not a failure. 5. Say what the change will cause. Before making it, name the consequences seen: what else moves, breaks or goes stale, and what it costs. When a consequence makes the change a poor one, say so first and offer the better way; the author decides.

sections.name: Every state before done
sections.text: A piece of UI is not done when it looks right with the one text it was built with. It is done when it holds with every text and value it will be given. The agent tries those before saying "done", not the author after. It is one case of Consequences first. the close button pushed under a long alert message The alert above was built with a short message. A long one took the whole row, and the close button wrapped to a line of its own, under the text. One long message in a test would have shown it. Why The author sees the UI with real data, and real data is never the sample the agent typed: a name is long, a title is missing, a count is zero or a million. Each of those breaks a layout made for the sample, and each break costs the author a screenshot and a message. Trying the states takes the agent minutes; finding them one by one takes the author days. One alert in six states: the sample, too long, missing, tiny, absurd and error; in each the text wraps inside and the close button stays top right The rule 1. List the edge cases and the states before calling it done. The element's own states: loading, error, disabled, many at once. Then, for every text and value it shows, the edge cases: - too long: a title of three lines, a word with no spaces, a path, a URL; - missing: empty, null , no title at all; - tiny: one letter, one item; - absurd: zero, negative, a million, a date years away. 2. Render each one and look. A screenshot of each state, or one page with all of them side by side. A state that was not rendered was not tested. 3. Make the layout hold them. Fixed parts keep their place: a close button stays top right however long the text, a long text wraps or ellipsizes inside its own column, an empty one collapses or shows a placeholder. Nothing overlaps, nothing is pushed out of view, nothing shows through from behind. 4. Keep the states in a test. The crowded case goes into the e2e test (end to end: a browser opens the real page and acts as the user does), with an assertion that nothing overlaps, so the next change does not break it again unseen. 5. Report what each state led to. The reply names the states rendered, with the screenshots, and sorts them in two: - Decided, for your information. A state with a clear answer is handled and said: "a title longer than the row is cut with an ellipsis; the full one is in the tooltip". - Ambiguous, needs your confirmation. A state with no clear answer is not guessed at quietly. It is put to the author as one question with the options: "an empty title: hide the header, or show 'Untitled'?".

sections.name: Every point of view
sections.text: One task is several stories told side by side: how the user uses it, how it is built, how someone would break it. An agent tells each story before calling the work done, and the screen follows the user's story, whatever the implementation does inside. It is one case of Consequences first. Send is pressed: on the left the comment is nowhere for 2 seconds, then it shows; on the right it shows at once marked Sending, and the mark goes when the server has it Above, a comment sent under a task. In the implementation's story it goes to the server, waits until it is filed, and comes back with the next refresh, and that story is right. In the user's story they answered under this task, and for two seconds the answer is nowhere. Both stories describe the same click; only one was told while building it. Why An agent builds from the implementation's story, because that is the one it writes: files, queues, requests. The user lives in another story, of what they did and what they see, and the attacker in a third, of what they can reach. A defect in one story is invisible from the others: a correct queue is a missing message on screen; a convenient endpoint is an open door. The author finds each one by living that story, one message each. The points of view One task, send a comment, and the stories around it: the user's, the implementation's and the attacker's told by the author; the operator's, the next developer's and the newcomer's suggested by the agent Told by the author: - User. What I do, what I see, what I expect next. The screen answers my action at once, where I acted; the route inside is not my business. - Implementation. How it works: where data goes, in what order, what waits for what, what happens when a step fails. - Attacker. What I can reach, read, change or flood that I should not: an input, a URL, a file name, a message that is also an instruction. Suggested by the agent, for the author to confirm: - Operator. It failed at night and I have the logs and the data folder: can I tell what happened, and restart it without losing anything? - Next developer. I open the code a year from now: can I find where this lives, read why it is so, and change it without breaking the rest? - Newcomer. I see it the first time, with no context: does the screen say what it is, what to do, and what just happened? The rule 1. Tell each story before the first edit. One or two lines each, in the person's words: "I click, my answer is under the last message". A view that does not apply is skipped, not forgotten. 2. The screen follows the user's story. When the implementation takes a longer way (a queue, an inbox, a second agent), the user still sees the result where they acted, at once, marked as pending until the way ends. The route stays inside. 3. Each story gets its test. The user's story is an e2e test (end to end: a browser opens the real page and acts as the user does) of what the screen shows and when; the attacker's is a test of what is refused. 4. Report by story. The reply says what each view found, and what was changed for it, so the author need not read the work through each pair of eyes again.

sections.name: Data as a picture
sections.text: A reply that carries data shows it as a picture. The author takes in a shape at a glance, where the same data as a paragraph takes a minute and still hides how its parts connect. The agent asks what the data answers, picks the kind of diagram for it, and draws that. It is one case of Every point of view: the author's story is what they see. Six questions about the data, each with the kinds of picture that answer it: how it works, what it is made of, where it stands, what went wrong, how much and how often, what it changes Why An agent thinks in text, so it answers in text: steps as a numbered list, states as sentences, a plan as paragraphs, numbers in a row. The author has to rebuild the shape in their head: which step waits on which, where the failure was, what is done and what is not. A picture hands them the shape itself. Text that holds data is the author's work left undone. The rule 1. Find the data in the reply. Steps, calls, states, parts, links, a plan, a failure, numbers over time, a change: anything with a shape. 2. Ask what it answers, and take the kind the chooser below gives. Two questions, two pictures; never one picture that answers neither well. 3. Draw that kind as its page says, on the diagrams page: its parts, its colours, when it does not fit. 4. Picture first, words after. The reply opens with the outcome in a line, then the picture, then a line of what it shows; lists and logs come last. 5. Check it before it goes: every text inside its box, nothing on top of anything else, every arrow attached, words as big as the text around it, the colours of the page it is shown on. A picture that was not looked at was not checked. 6. No shape, no picture. One fact, a yes or no, a name, a single number: a sentence. Which picture for which data - How does it work? Steps, calls and decisions: sequence (who talks to whom, in order), flowchart (what is decided where), state (what it can be, what moves it), flywheel (what feeds itself, where it is slow), swimlanes (who does each step), pipeline (files in, steps, files out), call graph (which function calls which). - What is it made of, and where does it run? Parts and links: labelled diagram (one thing and its parts), containers (the parts of a system), cloud, tiers, network, isometric (where each part runs), entities (the data and its links), modules and matrix (which file or part needs which), data flow (where data crosses a trust boundary). - Where does it stand? Progress and plans: milestone (one goal), kanban (many pieces of work), plan graph (what waits on what), roadmap (what is planned when), dashboard (many parts at once), versions (which version runs where). - What went wrong, and why? A failure, a log: timeline (what happened when), chronology (what one user did, in order), cause tree (why), one case (one request, today beside fixed), questions (what is known and what is not), waterfall (where one request spends its time). - How much, how often? Numbers: line chart (over time), heatmap (which days and hours), event plot (every event of many actors, at its time), sankey (where it goes, how much), service map (what talks to what, live), flame and treemap (where the time or the size goes). - What does it change, and what first? screen (where on the screen), screenshots before and after (what the author sees), change map (which files), quadrant (what to do first).

sections.name: Sequence diagram: who talks to whom
sections.text: The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change. Its parts: participants with an icon above the name, dashed lifelines under them, messages as arrows top to bottom; blue a request, green a success, red a failure, grey what stays the same Fits when - Parts pass something along: a person, a browser, a server, a database, a job, an outside service. - The order matters: a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens where, and after what. - A fix changes the course: a step added, an event dropped, a call moved. Today beside proposed. Not when - One part alone, nothing passed between: its states are a state diagram, its decisions a flowchart, its look a screenshot. - The order does not matter, only where the parts run or how the data links: a container sketch or an entity-relationship diagram. - The times matter more than who: a timeline. - Too many at once: more than five participants or ten messages. Split it in two, or say it in a table. - A change the author sees on screen: screenshots before and after say it better. How it is drawn 1. Participants: one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of the reading; the names stay short. 2. Lifelines: a dashed vertical line under each participant. 3. Messages: arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its arrow: 13:05 INSERT … SELECT , 403 plan limit . 4. A step on a clock or a loop (every minute, a retry until it works): a low rectangle with well-rounded corners (48 high for 18-pixel words, its radius a third of that), spanning the lifelines it involves. One arrowhead sits on its top edge pointing right, one on its bottom edge pointing left, so it reads as a cycle. Its period is written inside ( every minute ); what it checks and does goes beside it, right of the lifelines: alive? writing? , then gone, silent 30 s or older: started again . The loop is orange, the waiting colour; its words keep the usual text colours. Turned down: a straight arrow reads as one call, not a repeat; an ellipse reads poorly; a UML loop frame around the steps, its tag in the corner, stretches a compact diagram into a long one. A refresh sign, a filled rectangle with an arrow on every side and a path out of a lifeline and back came second. 5. Today beside proposed (or before beside after, today beside made): two framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed out, a step added, a participant greyed. 6. Around it: a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels. 7. In the app's colours, and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words no smaller than the text around it. S4, a plan limit: today the browser sends an error event to the tracker after the upgrade window; proposed, no event Examples servermon kept running by the agent: systemd starts the agent, the agent writes and starts servermon, which writes a JSON line a second and keeps running when the agent restarts; every minute, in an orange rounded loop, the agent asks alive? writing? and starts it again if gone or silent 30 s U2, an upload retried: before, a passing 500 fails the export; after, the job waits and puts the file again, and the export is done D1, a deadlock in a cronjob retried inside the run: today an error event and the rows a run later; made, once more at once and no event D1, the same deadlock with no change proposed: the retry drawn as what would be done only if it grows E7, the exporter's upload: today a failed upload is an error event; proposed, retried up to 3 times, the file arrives, no event One upload through a render service: the browser gets a signed URL from the API through Cloudflare, puts the file straight to S3, asks for a render; the API queues it and answers 202; later SQS starts Lambda, which renders to S3 and marks the job done

sections.name: One case: today beside fixed
sections.text: One real request, its answer today beside its answer with the fix: the question on top, two framed panels under it, red for today and green for the fix. Big numbers and what works and what is missing follow, so the one case stands for the rest. A shop's help chat asked how much shipping to Canada is: today a vague reply, not covered; with a shipping-rates article, a table of four rates, answered; then the numbers, what works and what is missing, by effort Fits when - One real request shows the gap: a question a help chat cannot answer, a call that fails, a search that finds nothing. - The fix is content or data, and its effect is the answer itself: a table, a value, a reply. - The author must decide what to do next: the case convinces, the lists say what else is open and what each costs. Not when - The course of messages between parts changes, not the answer: a sequence diagram, today beside proposed. - Many parts at once, each with its state: a status dashboard. - A change on screen: two screenshots, before and after. How it is drawn 1. The question: quoted big in a soft blue box, where it was asked and when in grey beside it. The real words, not a summary. 2. Today: a red frame, a red cross in a circle and "Today:" with why it fails; inside, the real answer as given and a red tag ("not_covered"). 3. With the fix: a green frame, a green tick and "With" and the fix; inside, the answer it would give and a green tag ("answered"). Values go in a small table, a line between rows. 4. A verdict under each: in bold, red or green, what the panel shows; a line under it says where the real answer was seen, or in amber what is still to confirm. 5. KPI cards: four big numbers for the whole, each a few words of what it counts; red or amber for a count that stands for a gap. 6. Two lists: "Works" with green ticks; "Missing, by effort" with a pill per item, red for work to do (small, medium), amber for what waits on an answer (wait, check, decide). The item the case is about first, in bold. 7. Ticks and crosses are drawn as paths, not typed as glyphs, so every font shows them alike.

sections.name: Annotated screen: where on the screen
sections.text: A plain sketch of a screen, grey blocks and a few real labels, with an amber number on each spot that changes; beside it a numbered list says what changes at each. The reader sees where the change is before reading what it is. The checkout page sketched twice, while paying and with the card declined, in grey blocks with real labels for Checkout, the total of $84.00, the coupon field and the Pay button; amber number 1 sits by the coupon field under the total, 2 by the Pay button, faded, with a spinner and the word Paying, 3 by a red Card declined message right above the blue Pay button; beside the sketches a list says 1 the coupon field moves from the top of the page to under the total, 2 Pay shows a spinner and stays disabled until the bank answers, 3 the error shows right above the button, not at the top of the page; a Now box sums up the three changes Fits when - A change to a screen: a field moves, a button gets a new state, a message shows in a new place. - The question is where: words alone would say "the error moves up" and leave the reader to guess from where to where. - No screenshots yet: the change is planned, or the screen is still being built. Not when - Real screenshots exist before and after: one case, the screenshots side by side. - The parts of a system, not of a screen: a container diagram. - A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram. How it is drawn 1. The sketch: the screen as a framed wireframe, its parts as plain grey blocks; only the parts that matter get real labels, such as the total, a field's placeholder or a button's text. 2. States: a frame per state when the change shows in one state only, such as while paying or after an error; the state's name in bold above its frame. One frame when the state does not matter. 3. The numbers: an amber circle with a number beside each spot that changes, in the margin of the frame, never over a label; each number once only, in the frame where it shows best. 4. Colour in the sketch: grey for what stays; the changed parts in their real colours, such as a blue button or a red error. 5. The list: beside the sketch, the same amber numbers in order, each with what changes in bold and a line or two of why under it. 6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence all the changes together.

sections.name: State diagram: what moves a thing between its states
sections.text: The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says what moves it. A sign-in card: from signed out through the code and the wait to saved; a refused code goes back for a new link, an unread token is shown in its window Fits when - A thing has a few states, and the question is how it gets from one to another, or why it stays in one. - A state can be reached by more than one way, or left by a way that goes back. - A bug is a wrong state: stuck, skipped, or reached from where it should not be. Not when - The order of calls between parts is the question: that is a sequence diagram. - One decision with its answers, no lasting state: a flowchart. - More than about eight states: draw the part that matters, and say the rest. How it is drawn 1. States: rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean: blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that needs a look. 2. Transitions: the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout). 3. The start: a filled dot with an arrow into the first state. 4. Around it: a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one line under it saying how to read it.

sections.name: Flywheel: what feeds itself
sections.text: A loop that grows as it turns: each stage feeds the next, and the last feeds the first, so the next turn starts bigger. A data flywheel is the common case: use makes data, data makes a better model, a better model brings more use. Also called a virtuous cycle or a reinforcing loop. Search that learns from its users: more users, more searches, clicks logged, clicks as labels, model retrained and a better ranking, evenly on one circle, each with its number; clicks as labels in amber, only 15% usable, the weak link; seed labels by hand come in from outside Fits when - Growth feeds itself: more users bring more data, more data a better product, a better product more users. - The question is where it is slow: which stage holds back every turn after it. - A start from outside: what was put in by hand to get it turning, seed data or a launch. Not when - A thing goes round its states, nothing grows: a state diagram. - A step repeats on a clock (every minute, a retry): the loop on a sequence diagram. - How much each stage moves on: a sankey, its bands as wide as their share. How it is drawn 1. Stages: four to six boxes evenly on one circle, clockwise, the outcome on top; each with its name and its number now (40k a day). 2. Arrows: blue and bold, arcs of that same circle, each from one stage into the next; the last back into the first. Nothing bends off the circle: a wheel that wobbles reads as broken. 3. The weak link: the stage that turns slowest in amber, said in a line under the ring. 4. From outside: what started it or still feeds it, a grey dashed box with its arrow into the stage it feeds. 5. The middle: how long one turn takes.

sections.name: Flowchart: what is decided where
sections.text: The decisions one action goes through, in order: each question a diamond, each answer its own arrow, each outcome a box. What Paste decides: a token, running, this link; each answer leads to its own outcome Fits when - One action branches: a click, a request or a job that does different things depending on what it finds. - The question is which way it went, and why: an outcome nobody expected. - A rule has cases, and every case must be seen at once. Not when - A thing lives through states and comes back to them: a state diagram. - Several parts take turns: a sequence diagram. - More than about six questions: split it, or say it as a table of cases. How it is drawn 1. Steps: rectangles; the one that starts it darker. 2. Questions: diamonds, a few words ending in a question mark, the words inside the diamond. 3. Answers: the project's arrows, one per answer, each labelled (yes, no, or the value). 4. Outcomes: boxes coloured by what they mean: green done, orange refused or spent, blue the way on. 5. Left to right for the main way, down for the answers that leave it.

sections.name: Swimlanes: who does each step
sections.text: A process as its steps in order, a lane per actor, each step a box in the lane of who does it. An arrow leads from each step to the next, and it crosses lanes where the work changes hands. The reader sees who holds the work now and which hand-off waits on them. A refund in four lanes, Customer, Support, You the shop owner, and Payment service: the customer asks for a refund and support checks the order, both done in green; the amber arrow hands it to you, and Approves the refund is amber, waiting 2 days; then, dashed grey and still to come, the payment service pays it back and support e-mails the customer; a Now box says the refund waits on you to approve Fits when - Several people or services share one process, each doing a part of it in turn. - The question is who does what, and where the work passes from one to another. - A hand-off is slow or stuck, and the reader sees whose lane it waits in, often their own. Not when - Messages between parts of a system, in time order: a sequence diagram. - Decisions with yes and no branches: a flowchart. - A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram. - Many pieces of work by stage, not one process: a kanban board. How it is drawn 1. Lanes: one row per actor in one framed panel, the name in bold at the left, thin lines between the rows; two to five lanes, the reader's own named "You". 2. Steps: one box per step, left to right in order, each in the lane of who does it; a verb in bold and a few words under it. 3. Arrows: from each step to the next, down or up out of the box and then right into the next one; the arrowheads touch the boxes. 4. Colours: green for steps done, grey dashed for steps to come. A hand-off that waits on the reader is amber, its arrow too, and says for how long. 5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence who holds the work and what it waits on.

sections.name: Known and open questions: how it works, and the gaps
sections.text: How something works, stage by stage, with the facts read from the code and the questions no one can answer yet, each where it arises. A panel per stage, left to right; the questions inside the panel they belong to; a row of big numbers under them. Gift cards in a small shop: buying, spending and expiring as three green panels of facts; amber questions inside them, a refund, two orders at once, a return, a reminder, the law; 1 240 cards sold, 3 400 left unspent, 5 open questions, 0 reminders sent Fits when - Someone asks how a thing works, and part of the answer is "no one knows yet". - The facts and the gaps must be told apart: what the code says, beside what a person still has to decide or find out. - A meeting needs its questions: each one shown where it bites, not in a list at the end. Not when - What is decided where, step by step: a flowchart. - A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram. - Where many parts stand: a status dashboard. How it is drawn 1. The title says both halves: "how it works, and what we don't know", and the line under it says what green and amber mean. 2. Stages: a green panel each, numbered "1 · Buying", left to right, an arrow between them; a few short lines of facts, the key figures in bold. 3. Questions: an amber note inside the panel where the question arises, a thick amber bar on its left; the question in bold, and in grey what is known so far. 4. Big numbers: a row under the panels, each a number and two lines of what it counts; amber or red when it stands for a gap. 5. Facts only in green: a line in a green panel is read from the code or a log; a guess is a question, and goes in amber.

sections.name: Cause tree: why it happened
sections.text: The failure on top, its causes below it as a tree: each row down says why the row above happened. The root cause is amber, the fix green beside it, and the causes that were checked and ruled out stay in grey with the reason. The reader sees why it broke, what one change ends it, and what was already looked at. Why customers were charged twice: a red box on top says customers were charged twice, 38 orders on 10-14; below it, the pay button sent twice, two requests 0.4 s apart, beside two grey dashed boxes ruled out, the provider retried (one call each) and a reload resent it (no reloads); below that, the button stays enabled for the 1.8 s it waits, beside a grey box ruled out, the mobile app retried (all 38 on web); at the bottom the root cause in amber, the spinner shows only after the reply, joined by a green line to the fix, disable the button on the first click and show the spinner at once; a Now box says a second click gets through while the button waits Fits when - Something broke and the question is why, down to the one cause a change would end. - Several causes were suspected, and the reader sees which were checked and why they are out. - The fix follows from the cause, and the reader sees it is aimed at the root, not at the failure on top. Not when - The order of events in one request: a sequence diagram; what happened when, from a log: a timeline. - The cause is not found yet: what is known and what is still open, a questions diagram. - One real request today beside the same with the fix: a case. How it is drawn 1. The failure: a red box on top, what broke in a few words and, under it, how much or since when. 2. The causes: one box per row down, each the "because" of the box above it, its name in bold in two or three words and under it what shows it; dark lines join the chain from the failure to the root. 3. Ruled out: a grey box with a dashed border beside the cause it was checked against, its name in grey and "ruled out:" with the reason; grey dashed lines join it. 4. The root cause: the last box of the chain, amber with an amber border, its name in bold and "the root cause" under it. 5. The fix: a green box beside the root cause, joined to it by a green line, the change in bold. 6. Now: a blue box under the tree says in one sentence why it broke and what fixes it.

sections.name: Timeline: what happened when
sections.text: Events at their moments, from a log: one line of time, left to right, each event a dot with its time and a few words. A sign-in second by second: started, link opened, code typed, ended with the token unread, then Paste starting a new sign-in Fits when - A log tells it: times matter, and the gaps between them. - The question is what came before what, or what happened while something else waited. - One event went wrong among others that did not. Not when - Who sent what to whom matters more than when: a sequence diagram. - The times do not matter, only the order of states: a state diagram. - Hundreds of events: pick the few that tell it, and say how many were left out. How it is drawn 1. The line of time: one grey line, left to right. 2. Events: a dot on the line, a stem to its label, the time in bold above a few words. The labels go above and below in turn, so close events do not collide. 3. Colours: blue for what went as it should, green for an end that is wanted, red for what went wrong. 4. What went wrong gets a note of its own, in red, under its event.

sections.name: Chronology: what one user did, in order
sections.text: Steps in the order they happened, each with its time, at even distances: the order and the times count, not the gaps between them. A long gap is cut short, its length written on the cut. One user's seven steps evenly along a line, from opening the pricing page on Monday to upgrading to Pro on Tuesday, the 23-hour night cut short For more steps than a strip holds, the same chronology goes down a line, the times on the left, one row per step. The same seven steps as a list down a vertical line, the times on the left, the 23-hour night cut short between the fifth and the sixth Fits when - One actor's steps: a user, a job, an agent; first this, then that. - The order matters more than the distances: a minute and a night between two steps take the same room. - Steps far apart in time: minutes, then a day, then a week; a timeline would squeeze the short ones flat. Not when - The gaps are the story: a wait, a timeout, what happened while something else waited: a timeline. - Several parts pass something between them: a sequence diagram. - The states matter, not the steps: a state diagram. How it is drawn 1. The line: one grey line, left to right in the strip, top to bottom in the list. 2. Steps: a dot each, at even distances. In the strip, a stem to its label, the time in bold above a few words, the labels above and below in turn; in the list, the time on the left, the words on the right. 3. Colours: blue for each step, green for the end that is wanted, red for a step that went wrong. 4. A long gap: the line cut by two slanted amber strokes, its length written in amber on the cut. 5. Strip or list: a strip up to seven or eight steps; more, the list.

sections.name: Event plot: who did what, when
sections.text: Every event of many actors at its moment: a lane per actor, a tick per event at its time, coloured by its kind. Also called a raster plot; told as a timeline, a swimlane timeline. Who did what today: a lane per account, a tick per save, rename, export, delete or sign-in from 08:00 to 20:00; the busiest account works in bursts all morning, health checks tick evenly all day in a lane of their own Fits when - Many actors, one log: accounts, users, jobs or services, each with its events over the same hours. - When and by whom matter together: bursts, quiet hours, who works when, what one actor did before another. - Every event counts: a single delete in a lane of saves shows as one red tick. Not when - One actor's steps: a chronology, or a timeline when the gaps matter. - Only how many, by hour and day: a heatmap counts them in cells. - What each actor sends the others: a sequence diagram. How it is drawn 1. Lanes: one per actor, its name on the left; the busiest on top. 2. The time: one axis under the lanes, thin grey lines at even hours. 3. Ticks: a thin bar per event at its time, coloured by its kind, a legend of the kinds on top. 4. Totals: at the end of each lane, how many events it holds. 5. Noise: health checks, bots, staff in a lane of their own, under the rest; the many quiet actors folded into one lane, "31 other accounts".

sections.name: Milestone track: where a goal stands
sections.text: One goal and its steps on a line, left to right: the steps done, the step now, the steps ahead, and who each one waits on. Payments open to every shop, 3 of 6 done: the card form, refunds and five shops trying it done with their dates; fees shown at checkout now, waiting on you to approve the text; opening to every shop by you and watching the first week by me ahead Fits when - One goal, a few steps: four to seven, each done or not. - The question is what is next and who it waits on: the reader or the agent. - The same track is shown again later, and the reader sees how far it moved. Not when - What happened when matters, not what is left: a timeline. - A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram. - Many parts at once, each with its own state: a status dashboard. How it is drawn 1. The band: one framed panel; a flag, the goal's name in bold and how many steps are done, in blue, beside it. 2. The steps: dots on one line, left to right. A done step is green with a tick, a green line up to the step now; the step now is a blue ring with its number; the steps ahead are grey, numbered, on a grey line. 3. Under each dot: its name in a word or two, and under that its date when done, or who it waits on: "waits on you" in amber for the step now, "by you" or "by me" for the steps ahead. 4. Now: a blue box under the line names the step now and what it waits on, in one sentence.

sections.name: Plan graph: what waits on what
sections.text: A plan's parts as boxes, an arrow from each part to the parts that wait on it. Parts that can run side by side stand in one column. The longest chain is bold blue: it sets the day the plan ends. A coupon field at checkout in five parts over seven days: P1 the coupon API, 2 days, done in green; then side by side P2 the form, 3 days, under way in blue, and P3 the e-mail, 1 day, not started in grey; both lead to P4 tests, 1 day, not started; then P5 your go, waiting on you in amber; the arrows P1 to P2 to P4 to P5 are bold blue, the longest chain; a Now box says a late form moves the ship day, the e-mail can slip 2 days, and then it waits on your go Fits when - A plan in parts, some of which wait on others and some of which can run at the same time. - The question is what holds the end date: which parts must not slip, and which have time to spare. - A part waits on the reader, and the reader sees how much waits behind it. Not when - One goal's steps in a line, one after another: a milestone track. - The months ahead, bars against dates: a roadmap. - Work by stage today, not by what it waits on: a kanban board. - What is decided where, questions and their answers: a flowchart. How it is drawn 1. The parts: one box per part, its name in bold, P1, P2 and so on with a few words; under it how long it takes and where it stands. Three to eight parts. 2. The columns: left to right in the order the parts can start, the days on top. Parts that can run side by side are stacked in one column. 3. The arrows: from a part to each part that waits on it, from box edge to box edge, thin grey. 4. The longest chain: its arrows bold blue, so the reader sees which parts move the end date and which can slip. 5. Where each stands: green is done, blue under way, grey with a dashed border not started, amber with "waits on you" a part the reader must do or approve. 6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what holds the end date, what has time to spare and what waits on the reader.

sections.name: Roadmap: what is planned when
sections.text: The months ahead on one line of time, a lane per area of work, each piece of work a bar from its start to its end; a red line marks today. The reader sees what is done, what is under way, what is at risk and what comes next. The shop from July to December: Payments has the card form done and bank payouts under way; Checkout has Apple Pay under way and tax by country at risk in amber after it; Help centre has the gift card articles done and search planned in grey; a red dashed line marks today, 10-16; a Now box says tax by country is at risk because it needs Apple Pay Fits when - Several areas of work over months: what each one does when, side by side. - The question is what comes next and what is late, measured against today. - One piece of work waits on another, and the reader sees the delay push the next one. Not when - One goal and its steps, done or not, no dates ahead: a milestone track. - Work by stage today, not by month: a kanban board. - What already happened, from a log: a timeline. How it is drawn 1. Time: the months left to right in one framed panel, their names on top; four to twelve of them. 2. Lanes: one row per area of work, its name in bold on the left, thin lines between the rows; two to five lanes. 3. Bars: one per piece of work, from its start to its end, its name inside in two or three words. Green is done, blue under way, amber at risk with its name in amber, grey with a dashed border planned. 4. Today: a red dashed line down the panel, behind the bars, its date on a red pill at the bottom. 5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what is under way and what is at risk, and why.

sections.name: Kanban board: where each piece of work is
sections.text: Many pieces of work at once, each in the column of its stage: to do, doing, in review, done. The board says what is in flight, where work piles up, and what waits on whom. The checkout's work this week: To do holds saved cards, the receipt e-mail and the coupon field, one more hidden; Doing is full at 3 of 3, Apple Pay, tax by country, and bank payouts blocked for 3 days in red; Review holds the fees text, waiting on you in amber; Done holds the card form and refunds with their dates, three more hidden; a Now box says what is stuck Fits when - Many pieces of work at once, each in one stage, none of them the whole goal. - The question is what is in flight: what is stuck, what piles up before a stage, what waits on the reader. - A stage has a limit, and the reader sees it is full before more work is started. Not when - One goal and its steps in order: a milestone track. - A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram. - Parts of a system and their health, not work to do: a status dashboard. - What happened when: a timeline. How it is drawn 1. The columns: one framed column per stage, left to right in the order work moves; three to five of them. 2. The header: the stage's name in bold, its count at the right. A stage with a limit shows "3 of 3" in blue when full; red when over. 3. The cards: one per piece of work, its name in bold in two or three words, under it who it is by and how long it has been there. 4. What stands out: a card that waits on the reader is amber with "waits on you"; a blocked card has a red border and says for how long; a done card has a green tick and its date. 5. Long columns: a few cards are shown, the rest as "+ 3 more" under them; Done shows the newest first. 6. Now: a blue box under the board says in one sentence what is stuck and what waits on whom.

sections.name: Priority quadrant: what to do first
sections.text: Many pieces of work weighed on two things only: how much each is worth and how much it costs. Value goes up, effort goes right, and the square splits in four quarters: do first, plan, later, skip. The reader sees what to start with and what to drop. Eight checkout ideas on value and effort: the green Do first quarter, high value and low effort, holds Apple Pay and saved cards; the blue Plan quarter, high value and high effort, holds the one-page checkout and tax by country; the grey Later quarter, low value and low effort, holds the coupon field and the receipt e-mail; the dashed grey Skip quarter, low value and high effort, holds dark mode and gift wrap as hollow dots; a Now box says Apple Pay and saved cards come first and gift wrap and dark mode are dropped Fits when - Many ideas and room for a few, and the question is which ones to start with. - Two things decide it: what a piece of work brings and what it costs, each a rough guess, not a measure. - The reader must say no to some of them, and wants to see why. Not when - Work by stage today, in flight or stuck: a kanban board. - The months ahead, what is planned when: a roadmap. - Options compared on many criteria, not two: a table, a row per option and a column per criterion. How it is drawn 1. The axes: value up the left side, effort along the bottom, each an arrow with its name; no numbers, only more and less. 2. The quarters: four framed boxes with a gap between them, each named in its outer corner in bold, what it means under the name. Do first is green, top left; plan is blue, top right; later is grey, bottom left; skip is grey with a dashed border, bottom right. 3. The dots: one per piece of work, where its value and effort put it, in its quarter's colour; a skipped one is hollow. Four to twelve of them. 4. The labels: the name in bold on its own light pill beside its dot, clear of the quarter's border and of other pills; right of the dot, or left when the right has no room. 5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what comes first and what is dropped.

sections.name: Container sketch (C4): where the parts run
sections.text: Which parts a system has, where each one runs, and what goes between them: the container level of the C4 model, drawn as a sketch. Where the parts of a notes app run: the app, its folder and an agent box on a laptop; a router and agent machines; model and speech services on the internet Fits when - The question is where: which machine, which box, which service runs a part. - Something crosses a boundary: a laptop to a server, a box to the internet, and what goes across. - A newcomer needs the whole before any one part. Not when - The order of the calls matters: a sequence diagram. - The data and how it links is the question: an entity-relationship diagram. - The inside of one part: its states or its decisions, a state diagram or a flowchart. How it is drawn 1. Where things run: dashed boxes with their names at the top left (a laptop, other machines, the internet). 2. Parts: boxes inside them, a name and one line of what each is; the one the reply is about in blue. 3. What goes between them: the project's arrows, grey, each with a few words. 4. Names: the standard ones from the glossary of names (laptop, router, vps1, box), never a private host. Examples A render service as C4 containers: a user, Cloudflare and Stripe outside; inside, the proxy, the API, the render queue, the renderer, the database, the cache and the media store, each with its technology and what it does

sections.name: Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links
sections.text: The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends. A note's data: a note holds messages, messages are linked in subjects, a message has files Fits when - The question is about data: where something is kept, what points to what. - A change touches a link: one becomes many, or a link goes away. - A newcomer reads the storage before the code. Not when - Where the data lives (which machine, which service): a container sketch. - What happens to one record over time: a state diagram. - Every field of every table: keep the main ones; the schema is in the code. How it is drawn 1. Entities: a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band, its main fields under it. 2. Links: plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has, linked in). 3. Their ends, crow's feet: two short bars across the line where it is one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or more). 1 and n in bold beside them, for a reader who does not know the marks. 4. Left to right in the order a reader meets them; a child under its parent.

sections.name: Status dashboard: where each part stands
sections.text: A RAG status dashboard (red, amber, green): the state of many parts at once, each a tile coloured by its state. Big numbers on top, the tiles grouped below, the gaps gathered at the end. Two more kinds at the end: tiles coloured by where each part is, and a whole beside its gap. The sign-in service: 4 of 8 parts in place, 212 unit tests pass, 1 browser test failed; providers and tests as tiles; the gaps, Apple's key, the browser test, the audit log and the docs, gathered at the end Fits when - The question is where things stand: many parts, each in place, stale or missing. - The reader must find the gaps fast: a project's checks, a release, an audit of what is covered. - The same view is read again later, and the colours show what moved. Not when - One thing and its states over time: a state diagram. - What happened in what order: a timeline or a sequence diagram. - A few parts only: a sentence or a list says it; a dashboard needs enough tiles to scan. How it is drawn 1. The key: green in place and checked, amber stale or unchecked, red missing or failed, in one line under the title. 2. KPI cards: three or four big numbers on top, each a word of what it counts and a line of context, coloured like the worst it stands for. 3. The status board: a panel per area, its name and a line of what it holds; a tile per part, its name in bold and its state in its colour. 4. The gaps: the amber and red tiles again, gathered in a panel at the end, so the reader does not hunt for them. 5. Real states only: a tile's word says why it has its colour ("1 failed", "no test"), never just "bad". Coloured by where it is When the question is where each part is, not how it is, the colours name places: production, development, the working tree. The list behind a tile opens on a click, in a panel beside the grid. The help centre's 12 topics: 7 on production, 4 on development not released, 1 only in the working tree; Coupons and Sizes with a red dot; Gift cards selected, its questions and sources in the side panel 1. A card per place, in the colour its tiles get: green, on production as it is; blue, on development and not released; amber, only in the working tree and not committed. 2. Each tile in the colour of its latest change: its name in bold, a small word for what is not out yet ("not released"). 3. A red dot on a tile: a question it cannot answer, its data missing. 4. The key under the grid, the red dot in it too. 5. Details on a click: the chosen tile gets a dark outline; the panel beside the grid shows its name, a tag of where it is, and short sections, headed in small caps, of a few bullets each. The tile never grows to hold its list. A whole and its gap When the question is how much is covered, one bar shows the whole and what is missing from it; a row of squares counts the runs. The help centre's 86 articles as one bar, 52 how-tos, 28 FAQs and a grey strip of 6, then a dashed red part for coupons and sizes; beside it 24 stories as squares, 19 passed, 1 failed, 4 skipped - The bar: a segment per kind, as wide as its count, dark green, light green, a thin strip for the rest. - The gap: a dashed red segment at the end, hatched soft red, its label on a pill: "+ coupons, sizes". - A grey line under the bar names the strip and the dashed part. - Units as squares, in rows: filled green passed, filled red failed, empty with a red outline skipped. A grey line under them says which failed, when, and why the rest were skipped.

sections.name: Line chart: a number over time
sections.text: One number over days or hours, a point for each, joined by a line; a dashed line marks the moment something changed, a deploy or a fix. The reader sees the number before and after, and whether it stayed. The checkout page's p95 load time from 10-01 to 10-14, a point a day, 0 to 3 s up the side: before the deploy the line is red at about 2.4 s, between 2.3 and 2.6; a blue dashed line marks the deploy of 10-08; after it the line is green at about 0.9 s, between 0.8 and 1.0; a grey dashed line marks the goal of 1.5 s; a Now box says the deploy cut p95 from about 2.4 s to 0.9 s, well under the goal Fits when - One number, measured again and again: a load time, an error rate, a queue's length; two numbers at most. - The question is before and after: did the deploy or the fix move the number, and did it stay moved. - A goal or a limit exists, and the reader sees which side of it the line is on. Not when - One run's time by function: a flame graph. - When something happens by hour and day of the week: a heatmap. - Work planned over months: a roadmap. - Events from a log, not a measured number: a timeline. How it is drawn 1. Time: left to right along the bottom, the dates or hours under it, every other one when they crowd; a week to a month of days, or a day of hours. 2. The number: up the side from zero, a few round values with their unit ("1 s", "2 s"), a thin line across the panel at each. 3. The line: a dot per measurement, joined. Red before the change, green after it when the number improved; one colour when nothing changed. 4. The change: a blue dashed line down the panel at its moment, its name and date on a blue pill at the top. 5. The goal: a grey dashed line across, its value at the right end; only when there is one. 6. What it says: the typical value before and after in the line's colour, next to the line, in a few words. 7. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what changed and by how much.

sections.name: Heatmap: when it happens
sections.text: A week in one grid: the days as rows, the hours as columns, each cell as dark as its count. The reader sees at once which hours of which days pile up, and which stay quiet. Checkout errors from 5 to 11 October, a row per day from Monday to Sunday and a column per two hours from 00 to 22; a legend scale runs from grey for none through five ambers to the darkest for 50 and more; most cells are pale, the weekend almost blank; a blue frame holds Monday to Friday at 08 and 10, every cell dark with its count inside, from 38 to 63; under the grid the hot spot is named, Mon to Fri 08:00 to 12:00, 493 of 684 errors; a Now box says 7 in 10 errors hit weekday mornings, while the late nightly import still runs Fits when - Many events, and the question is when: which hours of which days they come at. - A pattern repeats by the day of the week or the hour of the day, and a line of time would hide it. - One spot stands out, and its days and hours point at a cause: a job that runs late, a peak of visitors, a weekly report. Not when - One number over time, going up or down: a line chart. - Events in their order, each with its moment: a timeline. - Parts and their health, not the hours: a status dashboard. How it is drawn 1. The grid: in one framed panel, a row per day from Monday to Sunday, its name in bold on the left; a column per hour, or per two hours, its start on top. 2. The cells: one per day and hour, as dark as its count: grey for none, then pale to dark amber; five or six steps in all. 3. The scale: on the line under the title, a swatch per step with its range, from none to the darkest. 4. The hot spot: a blue frame around its cells, their counts inside them; under the grid, in blue, its days, its hours and its share of the whole. 5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence when most of it happens and why.

sections.name: Versions: which version runs where
sections.text: A table of what is deployed: one row per part, its version, its commit and its date, and whether it is the latest. A verdict in a sentence on top, what "latest" means at the bottom. What runs on production: api, web and worker run their latest release; the image resizer and the mail sender were deployed by hand, so no one can tell which code they run Fits when - The question is what runs now: before a release, after an incident, when a fix should already be live. - Some parts are deployed by hand, and the reader must see which of them no one can vouch for. - Many parts, each with its own version, too many to keep in mind. Not when - How the parts talk to each other: a containers diagram. - Where the parts run: a cloud diagram. - How healthy they are now: a service map or a status dashboard. How it is drawn 1. The time it was read, under the title: a version table is true only for the moment it was taken. 2. The verdict first: one sentence, its first half in bold, says what the table shows before the reader reads a row. 3. A row per deployed part: its name in bold, the version big and bold, the commit in the look of a link, the date. 4. Latest or not: a green tick and "latest", or an amber "? unknown"; never a guess. A grey note says why: "nothing on main is left out", or how it was deployed and the newest code there is. 5. What "latest" means, in a line under the table, and where it was read from. 6. The reader on top, agents below: the summary first; the sources of every version, the files and logs it was read from, go under a line, in a part of their own for agents.

sections.name: Cloud architecture diagram: what runs where
sections.text: The parts of a system inside the places they run: the internet, a CDN's edge, a cloud region, its network and subnets, the managed services beside it. Each part an icon with its name, the links as arrows. A render service on AWS: users and Stripe on the internet, Cloudflare at the edge; in the region a VPC with the load balancer and nginx in its public subnet, the API, PostgreSQL and Redis in its private one; SQS, Lambda and S3 managed, outside the VPC Fits when - The question is where: which region, which network, which subnet a part runs in, and what is managed by the cloud. - A link crosses a boundary: from the internet into the network, out to an outside service. - A design review or a newcomer needs the whole system on one page. Not when - What each part does matters more than where: a C4 container diagram. - Ports and who may connect: a network diagram. - The order of the calls: a sequence diagram. How it is drawn 1. The places: nested dashed frames, each named inside at its top left: the internet, the edge, the region, the network, the subnets. 2. Parts: a small icon over the name and one line of what it is. 3. Links: the project's arrows, coloured by kind (requests blue, data green, background jobs orange), a few words on the long ones.

sections.name: Network diagram: addresses, ports, who may connect
sections.text: The network engineer's view: address ranges as bands, the gateways at their borders, a security group around what it guards with what it lets in, every link with its protocol and port. The render service's network: a VPC of 10.0.0.0/16 with a public subnet for the load balancer and nginx and a private one for the API, PostgreSQL and Redis; each security group with its rule, each link with its port: 443, 80, 3000, 5432, 6379 Fits when - "Why can't X reach Y?": a port, a rule or a subnet in the way. - A firewall or security-group review: what is open, from where. - Addresses matter: ranges, gateways, what has a public address. Not when - What each part does: a C4 container diagram. - What data crosses where, for a threat model: a data flow diagram. How it is drawn 1. Bands: each subnet a filled band with its name and range. 2. Guards: a security group a dashed outline around what it guards, its rule on the outline ("5432 from sg-api"). 3. Links: every arrow with its protocol and port on a pill.

sections.name: Layered diagram: the tiers a request passes
sections.text: The parts in columns by tier, left to right in the order a request meets them: the edge, the entry, the compute, the background work, the data. The main path bold, the side paths in their own style. The render service in five tiers: Cloudflare at the edge, the load balancer and nginx at the entry, the API in compute, SQS and Lambda for background work, PostgreSQL, Redis and S3 as data; the main path blue, the render jobs dashed green Fits when - How deep a request goes: which tiers it crosses before an answer. - Where a part belongs: a new service placed in its tier, or one in the wrong one. - A caching or scaling talk: what each tier absorbs. Not when - Where things run, in which network: a cloud architecture diagram. - Many links between many parts: a dependency matrix. How it is drawn 1. Tiers: columns with a name and a line under it, left to right. 2. Parts: boxes in their tier; outside parties outside the columns. 3. Paths: the main one bold blue, the background one dashed green, the rest thin grey; a key under the drawing.

sections.name: Isometric diagram: the system as a model
sections.text: The same parts as blocks on an isometric floor, the networks as raised platforms, the main paths along the grid: a picture to point at on a slide, read before any word. The render service as an isometric model: users and Cloudflare on the internet; the region's VPC a slab with a platform for each subnet; the API, PostgreSQL, Redis and the replica on the private one; SQS, Lambda and S3 beside it Fits when - A slide or a talk: the whole system at once, for people who will not read a diagram's notation. - Groups matter more than links: what sits together on which platform. Not when - Exact links, ports or order: any other kind says it better; an isometric picture hides lines behind blocks. - The picture will change often: the layout is slow to redraw. How it is drawn 1. The floor: a faint isometric grid; places as dashed outlines on it. 2. Platforms: a raised slab per network, its name on a pill. 3. Parts: blocks for services, cylinders for stores, a name on a pill. 4. Paths: only the main ones, along the grid, coloured by kind.

sections.name: Service map: what talks to what, live
sections.text: What a tracing tool draws from real traffic: each service a circle with a ring for its health, each link as thick as its traffic, the numbers on the links. The unwell one stands out at a glance. The render service's map: Cloudflare 1000 requests a second, 300 through the load balancer and nginx to the API, 150 to Redis, 120 to the replica; Lambda ringed red with 3% errors, the replica orange with 0.4 s of lag Fits when - On call: which hop is slow or failing, and who depends on it. - Traffic matters: where the requests go, how many. - The real system, as measured, not as designed. Not when - The design, before it runs: a C4 container diagram. - How much of the traffic stops where: a Sankey diagram. How it is drawn 1. Services: circles laid out freely, an icon inside, the name and one number under it. 2. Health: the ring green, orange when slow, red when failing, dashed grey for what is not traced. 3. Links: thickness by traffic, "N req/s" on a pill; a legend.

sections.name: Sankey diagram: where the traffic goes, how much
sections.text: Traffic as bands that split and end, each as wide as its share: what a cache absorbs, what reaches each part behind it. 1000 requests a second reach Cloudflare; 700 are served from its cache, 300 go on through the load balancer and nginx to the API, which reads 150 from Redis, 120 from the replica, 30 from the primary Fits when - Capacity and cost: how much each layer absorbs and passes on. - A cache's worth: the share that never reaches the origin. Not when - Who calls whom: a service map or a layered diagram. - Flows too small to see beside big ones: say them in a line under it. How it is drawn 1. Columns: a thin bar per part, its name above. 2. Bands: from bar to bar, widths to one scale, each with its number. 3. Ends: what stops early ends at its own bar, in its own colour.

sections.name: Trace waterfall: where one request spends its time
sections.text: One request traced across services: a row per span, each a bar from its start to its end on one scale of milliseconds, a called span indented under its caller. The reader sees the slowest span, what runs in turn, and the gaps where the request only waits. A trace of POST /checkout, 1840 ms: the api's bar spans it all; under it auth checks the token in 40 ms, the cart service loads the cart in 240 ms with a database read of 180 ms indented under it, then an amber band marks 160 ms of waiting, then the payment provider charges the card in 1200 ms in red, the database saves the order in 80 ms and the mail queue takes the receipt in 30 ms; a Now box says the payment provider takes 1200 of the 1840 ms and 160 ms before it is a wait Fits when - "Why is this request slow?": one request, measured across the services it passes. - Calls in turn or at once: the reader sees what waits for what, and what could run side by side. - Time lost between spans: a gap where nothing runs is as plain as the work. Not when - The call stacks of one process, by function: a flame graph. - Who talks to whom, in order, with the messages: a sequence diagram. - A number over time, many requests: a line chart. How it is drawn 1. Time: milliseconds left to right in one framed panel, the ticks on top, faint dashed lines down from them; zero is the request's start. 2. Rows: one per span in the order it starts, the service in bold and what it did after it; a called span indented under its caller. 3. Milliseconds: each span's time in a column right before its bar, so the numbers read down one line. 4. Bars: one per span from its start to its end, to one scale; a few milliseconds still get a thin bar. The slowest span is solid red, its name and time in red. 5. Waits: a gap where no span runs is an amber band behind the rows, its length on an amber pill under them. 6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence where the time goes.

sections.name: Data flow diagram: where data crosses a trust boundary
sections.text: The threat modeller's view: outside parties, processes and data stores, the flows between them labelled with the data they carry, and the trust boundaries as red dashed lines. Each crossing gets a number to discuss. The render service's data flows: a user's login and cookie through Cloudflare into the VPC, banner JSON into PostgreSQL, render jobs to SQS, rendered PNGs to S3, a card token to Stripe; eight numbered crossings, three noted: TLS ends at the load balancer, the upload skips the WAF, only a token leaves Fits when - A security review or a threat model: each crossing is a place to ask what can go wrong (STRIDE per crossing). - Privacy: where personal data goes and what leaves. Not when - Ports and rules: a network diagram. - The order of one request: a sequence diagram. How it is drawn 1. Notation: outside parties as boxes, processes as circles, stores as two open lines; a key. 2. Flows: arrows named by their data ("card token"), not by protocol. 3. Boundaries: red dashed lines; a numbered badge where a flow crosses one, the risky ones noted under the drawing.

sections.name: Dependency matrix: every link in a grid
sections.text: The parts as rows and the same parts as columns; a filled cell where the row calls the column. Every link at once, however many, with no lines to cross. Twelve parts of the render service in a grid: users call Cloudflare on 443, the API calls Redis, PostgreSQL, the replica, SQS and Stripe; the one call below the diagonal, Lambda writing back to PostgreSQL, in orange Fits when - Many parts: where a graph turns into a hairball. - Layers and cycles: with the parts in order, a call below the diagonal goes against the layers. Not when - A few parts: a layered diagram reads faster. - The order of the calls: a sequence diagram. How it is drawn 1. Rows and columns: the same parts in the same order, the column names turned upright, groups bracketed on the left. 2. Cells: filled where the row calls the column, with a port or a verb when it fits. 3. Reading: a line under it says how ("the row calls the column").

sections.name: Call graph: which function calls which
sections.text: A program from its entry down: each function a box, an arrow to each one it calls, the related ones framed together, the helpers everything leans on at the bottom. bin/build from main down: the steps for the rules pages, the glossaries and the agents pages, each with its parser and renderer, all leaning on template_fill and html_escape; 16 of its 44 functions drawn, the rest as "+N more" Fits when - A change is planned: what calls the function, what it touches. - A newcomer reads a script: its steps and its shared helpers. - Dead code: a function nothing points at. Not when - Files, not functions: a module graph. - What the script reads and writes: a data flow of a script. - Where the time goes: a flame graph. How it is drawn 1. Layers: the entry at the top, each call one row lower. 2. Groups: light frames for the functions of one step. 3. Too many: the main ones drawn, the rest a "+N more" box.

sections.name: Data flow of a script: files in, steps, files out
sections.text: What a script reads on the left, the steps it makes of it in the middle, what it writes on the right; each arrow named by what passes along it. bin/build: docs/rules.md, the templates, the glossaries, the guides and the pictures in; parse, read guides, render and stamp in the middle; docs/rules.html and four more pages out, and the hand-written pages stamped in place Fits when - "Where does my edit end up?": from a source file to the page. - A build, an import, an export: a script whose job is files. Not when - The functions inside: a call graph. - A system of services: a layered diagram. How it is drawn 1. Files: a page icon and the path; inputs left, outputs right, the ones rewritten in place in their own colour. 2. Steps: rounded boxes in the middle. 3. Arrows: named by what passes ("Markdown", "index", "HTML").

sections.name: Module graph: which file needs which
sections.text: The files of a project as boxes in their folders, an arrow from each file to each one it requires, the packages from outside in their own shape. The rulebook's files: tests require src/make_rules_config.js and plugin.js, which require the rules and helpers; bin/build requires package.json and node-helpers and runs bin/self-check; the npm packages eslint, postcss and playwright below Fits when - What breaks when a file changes: everything that points at it. - Cycles and layers: an arrow that goes back up. - What a script drags in from outside. Not when - Functions inside one file: a call graph. - Hundreds of files: a dependency matrix. How it is drawn 1. Folders: dashed frames named at the top left. 2. Files and packages: a box with a folded corner for a file, a rounded one with a cube for a package. 3. Arrows: blue for a require, dashed orange for running it as a process; "+N more" for the rest.

sections.name: Change map: what a change touches
sections.text: The project's folder tree, trimmed to the files one change touches: each file a row, marked added, changed or removed, its lines added and removed at the right. The reader sees where the change lands and how big it is before reading the diff. The coupon field commit in the shop: on top 6 files, 3 added, 2 changed, 1 removed, +312 and −148 lines; under src/api, coupons.js added with +64 and old-discounts.js removed and struck through with −92, 4 more files folded; under src/checkout, checkout.vue changed with +18 −27 and coupon-field.vue added with +121; components, pages and store folded; tests/coupon.test.js added with +88; docs/coupons.md changed with +21 −29; bin and public folded; each file has a bar of green for lines added and red for lines removed; a Now box says it is mostly new code and checkout.vue is the file to check Fits when - One commit or one pull request: which files it adds, changes and removes, and where in the project they sit. - The question is where to look first: the big rows, the removed file, the one changed file in a folder of new ones. - A change spreads over folders: code, tests and docs, and the reader sees that each got its part. Not when - Which file needs which: a module graph. - How big each part of the code is, not what one change did: a treemap. - A script's data flow, files in and files out: a pipeline. How it is drawn 1. The total: on top of the panel, the number of files, then how many added, changed and removed in their colours; the lines added in green and removed in red at the right. 2. The tree: folders in bold with a slash, each level indented, thin grey lines from a folder to what it holds. 3. The files: one row each, a mark and its name in colour: green + added, blue ~ changed, red − removed and struck through. 4. The lines: at the right of each file, the lines added and removed as numbers, then a bar of green and red as long as they are. 5. What it leaves alone: folders and files the change does not touch fold into one grey row, "… 4 more files" or "… bin/, public/". 6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what the change is and which file to check first.

sections.name: Flame graph: where one run spends its time
sections.text: One measured run: each call stack a column of bars, the caller under the callee, each bar as wide as its share of the time. The widest bars at the top are where the time goes. One run of bin/build, 1531 ms: 889 ms waiting for bin/self-check, 363 ms in build_index_html, most of that reading whole images only to learn their size Fits when - "Why is it slow?": the time of a run by function, measured. - Before and after a speed fix: the same bar, narrower. Not when - The structure, not the time: a call graph. - Time across services: a sequence diagram of a trace. How it is drawn 1. Bars: bottom-up, the whole run at the bottom, widths to one scale, the name and the milliseconds in each. 2. Too narrow: a letter in the bar, its name in a key; a narrow part that matters zoomed above. 3. Self time: the bars that spend it themselves marked in orange.

sections.name: Code map: how big each part is
sections.text: A treemap of the code: each function a rectangle, its area its lines, grouped by the part of the program it belongs to. bin/build's 44 functions by size: the guides 184 lines, the glossaries 173, the indexes 157, the shared helpers 97; glossary_from_markdown the biggest at 76 Fits when - Where the code is: the big parts to split, the parts that grow. - A first look at a large file or project. Not when - Who calls whom: a call graph. - Where the time goes: a flame graph; size is not cost. How it is drawn 1. Groups: a frame per part, its name and its lines in the header. 2. Rectangles: one per function, area by lines, the name and the count when they fit. 3. The small ones: merged into a dashed "N small functions" box.

sections.name: Compact: one resource, every request a row
sections.text: A whole resource on one picture: each request a row, in the order they are sent, with what it sends, what it gets back and what the server keeps after it. Which request reads, adds, changes or removes, and what a repeat does, reads down a column. The articles API: GET the list, GET one, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, each a row with what it sends, its answer, the articles stored after it and what sending it twice does; a red line for an article that is not there Fits when - A resource and its requests: list, read, add, replace, change, remove; the reader learns the API, or checks what it does. - The difference between requests matters: PUT beside PATCH, POST beside PUT, what a repeat does. - The state after each request says more than its answer: what is added, replaced, gone. Not when - One request in detail, its headers and body, an error's answer: the expanded form. - The order of calls between parts, a server, a database, a queue: a sequence diagram. - Many resources at once: a compact picture each, or a matrix of addresses by methods. How it is drawn 1. A row per request, in the order they are sent, on a card of its own: the method as a badge, the address in a monospace font. 2. The method's colour says what it does to the data: blue reads, green adds, orange changes, red removes. A legend under the picture says so. 3. Five columns: the request; what it sends (a body in a code box, else "nothing"); what it gets back (the status in green, a line on the body); what is stored after it (each record a chip, the one touched in the method's colour, a removed one faded in a dashed red box); sent twice ("same", or what changes more in orange). 4. One small example of data runs through every row (articles 1 and 2, then 3 added, changed and removed), so each row's change shows. 5. What fails goes in a red line under the rows: a record that is not there, fields that are wrong, with their statuses. 6. Around it: a title with the resource, one line of how to read it.

sections.name: Expanded: one request taken apart
sections.text: One request and its answer, every part named: the method and address, the headers, the body, the status. Each part sits in a code box as it is sent, its name and what it is for beside it, so a reader learns what a request is made of and what to look at in one. A PATCH to article 3 and its 200 answer: method and address, headers, a body with only the title, then the status, headers and the whole article as it is now, each part named on the side Fits when - One request matters in detail: the one a bug is in, the one a client has to build, the one the docs explain first. - The answer has to be read: what the status says, what the body holds, how an error names the field that is wrong. - A newcomer learns the shape of a request once, to read the compact form after it. Not when - The whole resource, all its requests side by side: the compact form. - Parts talking to each other, in time order: a sequence diagram. - The difference is one field: the request and the answer as text, the field marked, say it better. How it is drawn 1. Two code boxes, the request on top and the answer under it, each in its parts as they are sent: the first line, the headers, the body. A dashed line between the parts. 2. The name of each part beside it, on a coloured bar: the method's colour on the method and address, green on a status that worked and red on one that failed, blue on a body, grey on headers. Under the name, a few words on what it is for in this request. 3. Real values, short: a token cut with "…", a body with only the fields that matter. 4. A failure is drawn the same way, the status and the body that names what is wrong in red, so the reader sees what a client gets back. 5. Around it: a title with what the request does, one line of what it shows. A POST with no title and its 422 answer: the status and an errors body naming the title as required, both in red

sections.name: A file has an address system.
