sections.text: Before reading a line, you should already know where dependencies, policy, behavior, helpers, and execution live. 01 / BIN #!/usr/bin/env node 02 / DEPS const cli = require('@vbarbarosh/node-helpers/src/cli'); const fs = require('node:fs'); 03 / POLICY const REPORT_LIMIT = 31; 04 / RUN cli(main); 05 / ENTRY function main() { // public behavior } 06 / HELP function format_percent(value) { return `${value}%`; } Dependencies are visible. require statements sit together and sort cleanly. Execution is announced early. After dependencies and policy, cli(main); says: start here. main owns orchestration. It is the first declaration and an exception to domain-first naming. Helpers explain downward. Each name encountered above can be resolved by continuing to read.

sections.name: Brace position reveals scope.
sections.text: The unusual part is intentional: module-level declarations form landmarks; nested behavior stays visually compact. Module scope brace moves down function main () { // top-level landmark } The brace creates a strong horizontal break before the file’s primary behavior. Nested scope brace stays put function main () { function limit_print (limit) { console.log(limit); } } Nested declarations, callbacks, and control flow keep the brace on the declaration line.

sections.name: Names tell you what will happen.
sections.text: A function is a verb phrase. Data is a noun phrase. The assignment reads like a small, testable sentence. Behavior Imperative verb markers announce an operation. users_group_by_role(users) function users_index_by_id(users) function items_sort_by_time(items) function → Result Noun shape and plurality announce what is stored. users_by_role Record<role, User[]> user_by_id Record<id, User> items_sorted_by_time Item[] const users_by_role = users_group_by_role (users); users Plural: one key can return many users. _by_role Data lookup: bracket access, or .get() on a Map; never a function call. _group_by_ Verb marker: this side performs the grouping.

sections.name: Watch the rules change the code.
sections.text: The result is longer by line count and shorter by interpretation time. Shape, mutation, and exit are all exposed. Before compressed decisions const group = (arr) => arr.reduce((acc, x) => { (acc[x.role] ||= []).push(x); return acc; }, {}); const result = group(users); module.exports = group; Applied each decision gets a line function users_group_by_role (users) { const out = {}; for ( const user of users) { out[user.role] ??= []; out[user.role].push(user); } return out; } module.exports = users_group_by_role;

sections.name: Imperative flow reads downward.
sections.text: No accumulator protocol to mentally execute. The loop says what exists, what is missing, what changes, and what leaves. INPUT Take users The plural parameter states the incoming collection. CONSTRUCT Create out The local return container has one conventional name. ITERATE Visit each user for...of and singular user expose cardinality. RETURN Return out The constructed result exits once, at the bottom.

sections.name: Objects carry only what crosses the boundary.
sections.text: Explicit construction makes the output contract reviewable. A spread silently couples it to every future source field. Implicit payload The output grows whenever item grows. return {...item, index}; uid parent_uid token debug index Declared payload The output changes only when this code changes. return {uid: item.uid, parent_uid: item.parent_uid, index}; uid parent_uid index

sections.name: The 30-second review. scan top → bottom
sections.text: 1 Can I identify the file type? A library ends with one export. A script hands main to cli(main); after globals. 2 Is the entry convention correct? A script declares main first; a library uses a domain-first function name. 3 Do names reveal data shape? Plurality, _by_ , and _sorted_by_ agree with the value. 4 Does control flow read downward? Guards return early; loops are explicit; deep pipelines are gone. 5 Is the constructed result named out ? The caller gives it the domain name after the function returns. 6 Are boundaries explicit? Dependencies, object fields, helpers, and execution are visible.

sections.name: Log line format
sections.text: [2026-08-17T02:55:07.000Z] [cd8e5vqp] [db_query_begin] name=select_users time ISO-8601 UTC, ms group_uid unit of work sender the one call site details terse, single line File [2026-08-17T02:55:07.000Z] [cd8e5vqp] [db_query_begin] name=select_users Docker [cd8e5vqp] [db_query_begin] name=select_users ← the runtime timestamps the line

sections.name: Legend
sections.text: [time] ISO-8601 UTC with milliseconds; dropped when a collector adds it group_uid one unit of work — request, job, cron run [sender] one call site, unique in the whole codebase group_spawn opens a group; parent= names the caller's group group_exit optional close; after it, no producer emits for that group _begin operation start _end_ok completed successfully _end_error completed with an error spawn relation — happened inside the parent group

sections.name: Rules
sections.text: A line carries time , group_uid , sender , details — nothing else. Elapsed time, status, and every other measurement belong in details . time is required when writing to a file, and omitted when the runtime already timestamps the line, as docker does. Every event belongs to a group: one request, job, or cron run. The uid is opaque, usually a cuid. A group opens with group_spawn , emitted synchronously before the uid is passed anywhere: [new_group_uid] [group_spawn] parent= old_group_uid Omit parent= for a root group. A receiver uses the caller's uid as the parent of its new group. sender identifies one logging call site. The name is unique in the whole codebase, so a grep lands on one place. It is snake_case and matches ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$ . A _begin event is closed by the same stem: _end_ok — completed successfully _end_error — completed with an error _end — the outcome itself, such as an HTTP status, already says what happened group_exit is optional and mainly detects leaks. Its absence makes no claim, and consumers must accept groups without it.

sections.name: Limits
sections.text: Try to keep one line under 2k UTF-8 bytes . A log line describes an event; it is not payload storage. details never contains a physical newline. Never in a line secrets and tokens signed URLs and URL query values request or response bodies, headers Log a reference to the payload instead of the payload.

sections.name: Visualization
sections.text: One lane per group_uid . group_spawn draws the parent → child arrow. An event sits on the axis at its own time. Suffixes give each lane its start and its outcome. A lane with no end event is still open — group_exit is optional.

sections.name: Tree view
sections.text: c1a0root group_spawn ├─ server_begin v1.2.3 port=8080 ├─ c7f3a91k group_spawn │ ├─ request_begin GET /api/users │ ├─ cd8e5vqp group_spawn │ │ ├─ db_query_begin │ │ └─ db_query_end_error │ └─ request_end_error └─ (no group_exit) Summary per group group_uid parent status duration children c1a0root — OPEN — c7f3a91k c7f3a91k c1a0root ERROR 30.014s cd8e5vqp cd8e5vqp c7f3a91k ERROR 30.001s — Every column here is read back from the lines themselves. A duration comes from the details of the closing event, never from a field of its own.

sections.name: Details: value encoding
sections.text: bare name=select_users exit=1 ETIMEDOUT 4.512s quoted "no space left on device" "line one\n" "" json {"beta":true} [1,2,3] null counted 3:[180,783,846] 2:["bar","foo"] 0:[] truncated {"name":"asparagus","qua...+4821 bare — a printable ASCII word without spaces, double quotes, backslashes, or square brackets. A bare value is exactly the bytes that were sent: it cannot span words, break the line, or mint a fake [tag] . quoted — every other string is JSON-quoted, so newlines and control characters are escaped, and an empty value stays visible as "" . json — arrays, objects, booleans, and null use compact JSON. counted — an unordered list is sorted and prefixed with its count. Ordered values are never sorted. truncated — truncation preserves valid UTF-8 and ends with the number of omitted bytes. After group_exit "After" means producer emission order — not timestamp, not collector ingestion order. Buffering may deliver an older event later; that alone is not an error. A parent may emit group_exit for work it abandons, such as a child that timed out. Cross-process detection needs preserved per-group order, a shared sequence, or another causal-order signal. Without one it is advisory.

items.name: Explicit rules take priority for new code
items.text: Follow the surrounding code only where no explicit rule applies. A new rule does not require rewriting existing code; that refactoring can happen separately. An explicit rule requires error : use function (error) in new code even beside older function (err) handlers. A written rule beside older code: the old handler keeps function (err), the new one is written function (error); rewriting the old is separate work docs/README.md

items.name: Unwritten conventions bind too
items.text: An unwritten convention is still a convention. File names, CSS classes, formatting and even attribute order follow the same systematic approach, even where it is not written down. No rule names it, yet every file in components/ is kebab-case: user-menu.vue follows them, UserMenu.vue does not; the same for classes, formatting and attribute order docs/README.md

items.name: An option is "value" and "label"
items.text: A selectable option is always {value, label} — value is internal, label is displayed. Select, dropdown, radio, tabs alike. {value: , label: } One list of {value, label} options shown as a select, radio buttons and tabs; the user reads Netherlands, the code sends country=nl value_label.md

items.name: Opposites come from the established pairs
items.text: req/res is Express-only; res/rej is valid for Promise executors, as are the full names resolve/reject . since/until is begin/end said of time. construct/destruct create/destroy open/close begin/end start/finish first/last next/previous get/put src/dest source/destination res/rej (Promise) resolve/reject req/res (Express) request/response setup/teardown push/pull enabled/disabled import/export since/until (time) Made-up pairs and the established ones they should be: begin/finish to begin/end, create/remove to create/destroy, open/shut to open/close; and the narrow pairs with where each holds docs/README.md

items.name: Functions are verbs; data are nouns
items.text: Functions are verb phrases, data are noun phrases. Each assignment reads as a sentence — the verb performs, the noun holds. const users_by_role = users_group_by_role(users); users flows into users_group_by_role(), a verb, which makes users_by_role, a noun; the line read as a sentence docs/README.md

items.name: The verb form marks function or data
items.text: English verb morphology is the marker. An imperative verb makes a function; a past participle makes data. Where there is no verb, a function marker — _from_ , _to_ , _of_ , check_ — makes a function. One exception: a linter rule's function is named after its rule id, as ESLint does, block_layout(context) for block-layout . items_sort_by_time(items) // function items_sorted_by_time // data items_sort_by_time(items), an imperative, is a function; items_sorted_by_time, a past participle, is data; with no verb, _from_, _to_, _of_ or check_ makes a function naming_markers.md

items.name: A bare "by" name is data, never called
items.text: A bare _by_ name is always data, never a function: it is read with brackets, or with .get() when it is a Map — never called. user_by_id& 91;id] ✓ right user_by_id.get(id) ✓ right, a Map user_by_id(id) ✗ wrong user_by_id as a table of ids and users: read with brackets or .get(), never called docs/README.md

items.name: The first word's plural states what a key returns
items.text: Plurality of the first word states lookup cardinality — what one key returns, not how big the container is. user_by_id& 91;id] // User users_by_role& 91;role] // User& 91;] children_by_parent_id& 91;parent_id] // Node& 91;] user_by_id returns one User per key; users_by_role and children_by_parent_id return a list per key var_names.md

items.name: "Sorted by" is the same data, reordered
items.text: _sorted_by_ marks data of the same shape, reordered. The participle survives here because it carries what shape alone cannot. items_sorted_by_time // Item[], still an array four items by time, and the same four reordered as items_sorted_by_time, still an array naming_markers.md

items.name: _per_ marks a ratio or a rate
items.text: clicks_per_visit 1 240 clicks over 400 visits make clicks_per_visit, 3.1: a rate, not a list naming_markers.md

items.name: Group by, sort by, index by produce them
items.text: The operations that produce those shapes are _group_by_ , _sort_by_ and _index_by_ . The criterion follows the verb. users_index_by_id(users) // user_by_id users_group_by_role(users) // users_by_role items_sort_by_time(items) // items_sorted_by_time users_index_by_id() makes user_by_id, users_group_by_role() makes users_by_role, items_sort_by_time() makes items_sorted_by_time docs/README.md

items.name: "From" means computed: result first, source last
items.text: Use _from_ only when something is computed, parsed or constructed — result first, source last. user_from_token(token) date_from_timestamp(ts) tree_from_array(rows) a token is parsed into a User: user_from_token, the result first and the source last docs/README.md

items.name: _from_ never means lookup
items.text: A lookup disguised as construction is wrong. user_from_id(id) ✗ wrong user_by_id& 91;id] ✓ right ![an id looked up in the user_by_id table: user_by_id[id] is right, user_from_id(id) dresses the lookup as construction](../img/rules/from_is_not_lookup.svg) naming_markers.md

items.name: "To" belongs in method position
items.text: A standalone conversion prefers _from_ ; _to_ is for method position, where the source is the receiver. tree.to_json() tree.to_json() with tree as the receiver; standalone it is json_from_tree(tree), never tree_to_json(tree) naming_markers.md

items.name: No "to" in data names
items.text: _to_ is banned in data names — id_to_name is only a second spelling of name_by_id . id_to_name ✗ banned name_by_id ✓ right a map from ids to names is name_by_id; id_to_name is a second name for the same map naming_markers.md

items.name: No "indexed by"; bare "by" says it
items.text: _indexed_by_ does not exist. Bare _by_ already names that shape. users_indexed_by_id ✗ does not exist user_by_id ✓ right users_index_by_id() makes user_by_id; users_indexed_by_id does not exist naming_markers.md

items.name: "Grouped by" only for invariant plurals
items.text: _grouped_by_ is retired from data names except for invariant plurals — fish , data , series — which cannot state cardinality by plurality. Prefer a countable noun when one exists. fish_by_tank // Record<tank, Fish fish_grouped_by_tank // Record<tank, Fish& 91;] rows_by_source ✓ over data_by_source fish_by_tank returns one Fish, fish_grouped_by_tank a list; rows_by_source is preferred over data_by_source var_names.md

items.name: "Of" queries possession
items.text: _of_ is a possession query. descendants_of(node) a node and its five descendants in a tree, asked for as descendants_of(node) naming_markers.md

items.name: "is" names a boolean, a predicate or data
items.text: is_ names a boolean: a predicate that returns one, or data that holds one. It is not a function marker; a check that must read as a call is check_ , a verb. is_ancestor(a, b) // a predicate, called is_open // a boolean, read check_status() // a check that reads as a call is_ancestor(a, b) is called and returns true, is_open is read as false, check_status() is a verb that runs naming_markers.md

items.name: A conversion and its variable share a first word
items.text: A standalone conversion and the variable it fills share their first word. const json = json_from_tree(tree); const json = json_from_tree(tree): the variable and the conversion share the word json naming_markers.md

items.name: Names start with the domain
items.text: Naming is domain-first. Functions and files follow items_ , item_ or domain nouns; generic names are avoided. items_index_by_uid() ✓ right process() handle() util() ✗ avoid domain-first names such as items_sort_by_time() stand together; handle(), process() and util() say nothing FORMATTING.md

items.name: Verb-first families are the exceptions
items.text: The verb-first families are the exceptions to domain-first naming: main — reserved for the entry function of an executable script — format_ , render_ , export_ , is_ , refresh_ , click_ , emit_ , check_ (MP-40), make_ (MP-53), and the steps of a script ( build_glossaries_html() ). A step is a function main() calls once per part of the work, in order; a verb-first name that is not a step is renamed when next touched. function main() { report_print(); } main, format_ , render_ , export_ , is_ , refresh_ , click_ , emit_ , check_ and make_ start with their verb; main runs the steps of a script FORMATTING.md

items.name: A variable name states the shape of its data
items.text: users // User& 91;] user_by_id // Record<id, User users_by_role // Record<role, User& 91;] items_sorted_by_time // Item& 91;], reordered Four names and the shapes they state: users a list, user_by_id one User per id, users_by_role a list per role, items_sorted_by_time the same list reordered var_names.md

items.name: Name the result out
items.text: A variable the function builds and returns unchanged is named out — return out; , exactly. A parameter, a loop variable or an outer value returned unchanged keeps its own name: return user; . function emails_from_users(users) { const out = & 91;]; for (const user of users) { if (user.email) { out.push(user.email); } } return out; } emails_from_users builds out, pushes into it and returns out; returning a parameter unchanged as out is wrong, return user; is right return_out.md

items.name: out never leaves the function
items.text: The caller names the result by what it means. const emails = emails_from_users(users); const users_by_role = users_group_by_role(users); Inside emails_from_users the result is out; the caller names it emails return_out.md

items.name: Return a literal directly
items.text: Returning a literal or an expression directly is allowed; a guard return may return null , false , [] , {} . const out = {...}; return out; is rewritten as return {...}; const out = {a, b}; return out; ✗ rewrite this return {a, b}; ✓ as this const out = {a, b}; return out; rewritten as return {a, b};, and the guard returns null, false, () and {} FORMATTING.md

items.name: Errors use e in arrows, error in regular handlers
items.text: A caught error is error in a catch binding or regular function, and e in an arrow. This applies to promise rejection handlers and EventEmitter error listeners. Callback names stay e / error at every depth. DOM error events follow VAR-16; only nested catch bindings use numbered names (VAR-17). promise.catch(e = report(e)); server.on('error', function (error) { throw error; }); catch (error) { console.log(error.message); } An error is e in an arrow, error in a regular function and in a catch binding var_names_error.md

items.name: Reserve e for error arrows; no err or ex
items.text: e names an arrow error parameter. A regular error parameter or catch binding uses error , never e , err or ex ; only catch bindings get the nested numbers in VAR-17. catch (e) ✗ no catch (err) ✗ no catch (error) ✓ yes promise.catch(e = report(e)); ✓ yes catch (err), catch (ex) and catch (e) each rewritten as catch (error); e only in an error arrow var_names_error.md

items.name: Name stderr text by what it is
items.text: Accumulated stderr text is not an error variable. Name it by what it is. stderr ✓ right err ✗ wrong A child process writes stderr text, collected as stderr, not as err var_names_error.md

items.name: Prefer explicit temporaries
items.text: Use intermediate variables instead of nested expressions; favor clarity over terseness. A nested send(format_report(rows_filter(...))) rewritten as three named steps FORMATTING.md

items.name: Arrow values use v; arrow errors use e
items.text: A lone value or event parameter is v ; vv only when v is already taken where the arrow stands, vvv only when vv is. An arrow with no parameter, an error arrow or a parameter with another name takes nothing: () = items.filter(v = v.ok) , promise.catch(e = report(e, items.map(v = v.uid))) . A parameter the arrow does not use is not declared: promise.catch(() = items.map(v = v.uid)) , not e = … (LINT-03); a regular function may. Error arrows keep e at every depth (VAR-05). With several parameters, choose names for their roles; an error callback’s first parameter still follows the error naming rule. items.map(v = v.uid) items.some(v = v.sizes.some(vv = vv.width 100)) promise.catch(e = report(e)) Nested arrows name their value v, then vv only when v is taken, then vvv; an error arrow keeps e FORMATTING.md

items.name: The for...of loop variable is the singular of the collection
items.text: for (const user of users) { } for (const child of node.children) { } users gives user and node.children gives child; for (const x of users) rewritten as for (const user of users) for_of.md

items.name: A cached length is "end"
items.text: A cached array length in a single loop is named end . for (let i = 0, end = items.length; i < end; ++i) { } Six items, the index i and the cached bound end = 6, in for (let i = 0, end = items.length; i < end; ++i) for_i_end_ii_jj_kk.md

items.name: Nested bounds double the index: ii, jj, kk
items.text: In nested loops the cached bound is the doubled index name: i → ii, j → jj, k → kk. for (let i = 0, ii = foo.length; i < ii; ++i) { for (let j = 0, jj = bar.length; j < jj; ++j) { for (let k = 0, kk = baz.length; k < kk; ++k) { } } } Three nested loops: i with ii, j with jj, k with kk, each bound its index doubled for_i_end_ii_jj_kk.md

items.name: A transformed or conditional result is not "out"
items.text: Only that variable is out . A value that is joined, stringified or otherwise transformed on its way out, or returned only on a condition ( ?: , if ), is not out ; it is named by what it is. out returned on a condition and out joined on its way out, each beside the same code with a name of its own; below, the one right shape: built, then return out; return_out.md

items.name: Start time is "time0"
items.text: The variable holding the start time of a measurement is always named time0 . The elapsed time is the current time minus time0 : a number, shown to a person only through format_duration (FN-02), never as ${Date.now() - time0}ms at the call site. $time0 = microtime(true); echo format_duration(microtime(true) - $time0); const time0 = Date.now(); console.log(format_duration(Date.now() - time0)); time0, the work, Date.now() - time0, then format_duration gives 2m 35s; a hand-rolled ms string rewritten as format_duration var_names_time0.md

items.name: Use time0 for measurement; paired names for other roles
items.text: Do not name an elapsed-time start begin , start or t0 . Outside that role, use start/finish or begin/end when the pair is actually used. const time0 = Date.now(); // elapsed-time measurement const start = range.start; const finish = range.finish; A measurement start named start rewritten as time0; a range keeps start and finish or begin and end var_names_time0.md

items.name: Events use v in arrows, event in regular functions
items.text: A DOM event is a value, including an event whose type is error . A one-parameter arrow uses v ; a regular event handler uses event . Reserve e for error values in arrows. el.addEventListener('click', v = v.stopPropagation()); el.addEventListener('error', v = report(v)); el.addEventListener('error', function (event) { report(event); }); A click or error event is v in an arrow and event in a regular function var_names_event.md

items.name: Nested catch bindings use error2, error3
items.text: A catch inside another catch names its binding error2 , the next level error3 . This applies only to catch bindings: callback parameters stay e in arrows and error in regular functions, even inside a catch. catch (error) { try { await save_backup(scene); } catch (error2) { } } A catch inside a catch binds error2, the next error3; callbacks stay e or error var_names_event.md

items.name: A generic name has one meaning
items.text: i , j , k , end , ii , v , e , error , event , out , time0 , req , res and rej each have the meaning listed on one page, res one in each of its pairs, req/res and res/rej ; anywhere else the variable is named by what it holds. const out = & 91;...new Set(tags)]; return (out.length === tags.length) ? tags : out; ✗ no const unique_tags = & 91;...new Set(tags)]; return (unique_tags.length === tags.length) ? tags : unique_tags; ✓ yes The generic names and their meanings, res in both its pairs; out returned on a condition rewritten as unique_tags generic_names.md

items.name: A configuration value at the top is UPPER_CASE
items.text: A constant the module keeps as configuration, a global name for a value set in the code, is written in upper case at the module's top level. A const inside a function or a block is lower case. Imports are not this rule. const PRESS_MS = 400; // the module's top function press_start(event) { const started = Date.now(); // inside } PRESS_MS and BLOB_URL at the module's top in upper case; started and target inside a function in lower case MANUALLY_APPROVED_RULES.md

items.name: "format" strictly returns human-facing text
items.text: format_ returns a string to show to a person, including when the value comes from object state. format_bytes(1457664) // "1.4 MB" format_duration(155000) // "2m 35s" format_usd(1299) // "$12.99" format_bytes, format_duration and format_usd turn values into the strings a person reads format_xxx.md

items.name: "render" constructs asset content
items.text: render_ constructs content such as CSS, HTML or SVG from state. The result can be a string; its purpose is an asset rather than a human-facing formatted value. public function render_css(): string { return "body { color: {$this- text_color}; }"; } render_css and render_svg turn state into CSS and SVG assets render_xxx.md

items.name: Never hand-roll a display conversion
items.text: A display conversion is never hand-rolled at a call site — an inline one is a missed format_ . ${Math.round(bytes / 1024)}kB ✗ missed call format_bytes(bytes) ✓ right Three hand-rolled byte conversions giving three answers, each rewritten as format_bytes(b) giving 1.4 MB format_xxx.md

items.name: format_* returns — it never prints
items.text: Output is the caller’s job. console.log(format_tree(tree)); format_tree returns the text and the caller prints it; a format_tree that prints rewritten as console.log(format_tree(tree)) format_xxx.md

items.name: "format" is not serialization
items.text: format_ is not for machine formats. Serialization is conversion, not display. format_user(user) // "Alex K. (admin)" — humans json_from_user(user) // machines format_user gives the text a person reads; json_from_user gives the JSON a machine reads format_xxx.md

items.name: "render" is recomputed, never stored
items.text: The prefix separates constructed content from stored attributes. render_ is recomputed per call — never cached, never stored. $this- text_color // stored attribute $this- render_css() // constructed content A stored attribute is read; render_css is made on each call; storing its result rewritten as calling it where needed render_xxx.md

items.name: "render" may return null or throw
items.text: render_ may return null when not applicable, and may throw when the state makes the value meaningless. if (!$this- theme) { return null; } render_css returns CSS for a theme, null with no theme, and throws for a broken one render_xxx.md

items.name: "render" is sync and pure; downloads are "export"
items.text: render_ constructs content without DOM updates, file writes or downloads, and always returns its result. A function that brings a part of the page up to date returns nothing and is refresh_ (FN-10), never _render . A downloadable artifact — zip, csv or xlsx — is export_ , which may be async and side-effectful. $theme- render_css() // construct CSS content refresh_theme_labels() // bring a part of the page up to date export_zip() // produce a downloadable artifact render_css returns CSS, refresh_theme_labels updates the page, export_zip makes a download; theme_labels_render rewritten as refresh_theme_labels render_xxx.md

items.name: Format and render differ by output purpose
items.text: format_ returns a string a person reads; render_ constructs asset content. Both may return strings; reading object state does not turn display text into render output. format_bytes(1457664) // "1.4 MB", human-facing text $theme- render_css() // CSS asset content format_bytes returns text a person reads; render_css returns CSS a browser uses format_xxx.md

items.name: A local copy of remote data has "refresh"
items.text: Anything that holds a local copy of remote data has refresh() — it pulls the data and brings the local vars up to date. Mental model: the browser refresh button. refresh: async function () { await Promise.all(& 91; this.refresh_user(), this.refresh_photos(), ]); }, refresh pulls the remote data into the local copy, this.user and this.photos refresh.md

items.name: Refresh is safe to call anytime
items.text: refresh() is idempotent — safe to call at any moment, any number of times. refresh called on load, after a save and twice in a row reaches the same up-to-date state refresh.md

items.name: Refresh composes per-part refreshes
items.text: A fine-grained refresh_() syncs one part of the state; refresh() composes them. refresh_user: async function () { this.user = await fetch_user(); }, refresh runs refresh_user and refresh_photos, each filling its own part refresh.md

items.name: Init is the first refresh
items.text: mounted: async function () { await this.refresh(); this.ready = true; }, mounted awaits this.refresh(), then sets this.ready = true refresh.md

items.name: A modal returns a commit flag
items.text: An interaction — modal, popover — executes its own logic and returns a boolean commit flag. It expresses intent; it does not expose control flow. These are the best practices for vue-modal: modal.return(true) inside, await modal_x().promise() at the call site. // true → changes were committed // false → no-op (cancel, or no changes) if (await modal_upload().promise()) { await blocking(this.refresh()); } The caller awaits modal_upload; the modal does its own work and returns true, committed, or false, nothing to do interactions-should-return-only-boolean-flag.md

items.name: Guards return early
items.text: Validate inputs immediately and return null or empty values explicitly. The work buried in nested ifs rewritten as guards that return null and () first FORMATTING.md

items.name: One public value per library module
items.text: A reusable module exports one function, class, configuration or data value. Executable scripts export nothing; tool-shaped files follow the tool. format_bytes.js, Theme.js and config.js export one value each, bin/build exports nothing; a helpers.js exporting three values split into three modules FORMATTING.md

items.name: Four spaces, no tabs
items.text: Indentation is exactly 4 spaces. No tabs. A tab before const user turned into four spaces, shown as dots FORMATTING.md

items.name: A top-level function declaration puts its opening brace on the next line
items.text: function main() { } function main() { with the brace on its line, turned into the brace on the next line FORMATTING.md

items.name: Nested function: brace on the same line
items.text: A function declared inside another function keeps its opening brace on the declaration line. function main() { function limit_print(limit) { } } limit_print nested in main: its brace moves from a line of its own to the declaration line FORMATTING.md

items.name: Callbacks keep the brace on the line
items.text: Function expressions, callbacks and Promise executors keep the opening brace on the declaration line. server.on('error', function (error) { // ... }); return new Promise(function (resolve, reject) { // ... }); A callback and a Promise executor with the brace below, turned into the brace on the declaration line formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Class brace below; method brace inline
items.text: A class declaration puts its brace on the next line; its methods keep the brace on the declaration line. class Logger { constructor(parent_group_uid) { } write(format, ...values) { } } class Logger with its brace inline and a method brace below, turned into the class brace below and the method brace inline formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Always use braces
items.text: Always use braces for if , else , for , while . No single-line bodies. if (!user) return null; ✗ no if (!user) { ✓ yes return null; } if (!user) return null; on one line, turned into the same body in braces FORMATTING.md

items.name: else starts on a new line
items.text: if (a) { } else if (b) { } else { } else glued to the closing brace, turned into else if and else each starting a line FORMATTING.md

items.name: catch and finally start on a new line
items.text: try { } catch (error) { } finally { } catch and finally glued to the closing braces, turned into each starting a line formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Align "switch" and "case"
items.text: switch and case are aligned at the same indentation level. switch (type) { case 'voice': break; case 'text': break; default: } case and default indented one level under switch, turned into aligned with switch FORMATTING.md

items.name: Keep short objects on one line; expand only when needed
items.text: Multiple fields alone do not require line breaks. When size or nested structure requires a multi-line object literal, use one field per line and a trailing comma. const next = {uid: item.uid, parent_uid: item.parent_uid, index}; A short object broken over lines turned into one line, and an expanded object given its trailing comma formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Options-style methods are always function expressions
items.text: Even a return-only method without its own this or arguments keeps that form; the tiny-arrow rule applies to callbacks and value factories. const options = { refresh: async function () { }, px: function (value) { return value ? ${value}px : '0'; }, }; An options object with arrow methods, turned into the same methods written as function expressions formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Keep an expression on one line when it fits on one line
items.text: const total broken over two lines, turned into one line FORMATTING.md

items.name: Never break after "=" before a call
items.text: Never split an assignment after = when its right-hand side is a single function call. const users_by_role = users_group_by_role(users); ✗ no const users_by_role = users_group_by_role(users); ✓ yes const user = with the call on the next line, turned into one line FORMATTING.md

items.name: Break lines only to show structure
items.text: Break a statement only when its size or nested structure makes the break necessary. Line breaks must expose structure. A short condition broken for nothing turned into one line; a list of rows broken one row a line FORMATTING.md

items.name: A blank line marks a phase change — nothing else
items.text: Add one only when the following statement begins an independent conceptual step. Blank lines after every statement, turned into one blank line before the printing step FORMATTING.md

items.name: Keep setup next to its use
items.text: Keep setup adjacent to the loop, condition or call that immediately uses it. Tightly coupled setup and use are not separated merely because the statement type changes. const lines = () separated from its loop by a blank line, turned into right above it FORMATTING.md

items.name: Build objects from needed fields only
items.text: Construct an object from the required fields only. Do not spread a full object when a subset is needed. {...item, index} ✗ bad {uid: item.uid, parent_uid: item.parent_uid, index} ✓ good An object built by spreading the whole item, turned into one that names uid and index FORMATTING.md

items.name: Comment intent, not mechanics
items.text: Comments explain intent or policy only. No comments for obvious mechanics. One exception: the route comment of FMT-21 states the route. A comment repeating the call, turned into one giving the reason for the retry FORMATTING.md

items.name: Multi-line comments carry rules or guarantees
items.text: A multi-line comment carries a rule, an invariant or a guarantee. A three-line comment retelling the steps, turned into a two-line limit the function keeps FORMATTING.md

items.name: Every route has a route comment
items.text: Every route function carries a route comment directly above it: METHOD /path (params) . // Express route handler // GET /file/<name async function file_get(req, res) { } A route function with no comment, turned into one with its route comment, GET /file/ endpoint_comment.md

items.name: Parentheses only when the route takes input
items.text: Parentheses appear only when the endpoint takes input — body, headers, query, comma-separated, in that order. // Express route handler // POST /upload (body, header:x-filename) function upload_post(req, res) { } GET /health () losing its empty parentheses, and the upload route listing body before its header endpoint_comment.md

items.name: Headers prefixed; path params in the path
items.text: A header is prefixed with header: ; a path parameter is spelled in the path itself. header:x-filename /file/<name GET /file (name, x-token) turned into GET /file/ (header:x-token) endpoint_comment.md

items.name: An intent comment continues the same block on the next line
items.text: // POST /upload (body, header:x-filename) // Streams to data/ before the body is fully read. An intent comment split from the route comment by a blank line, turned into the next line of the same block endpoint_comment.md

items.name: Named functions outside class bodies are "function" declarations
items.text: Every named function outside a class — top-level or nested — is a function name(...) declaration. Class methods use their class syntax. function report_print() { } A function expression and an arrow held in const report_print, each turned into a function declaration FORMATTING.md

items.name: No spaces inside one-line braces
items.text: A single-line object or array literal has no space inside its braces or brackets — a standalone literal, a nested one, or one row of a list. { value: 'today', label: 'Today' } ✗ no {value: 'today', label: 'Today'} ✓ yes & 91; 'remote', 'host', 'service' ] ✗ no & 91;'remote', 'host', 'service'] ✓ yes An object and an array with spaces inside their braces, turned into the same with none FORMATTING.md

items.name: Parenthesize compound operands in logic
items.text: In a logical expression ( && , , ?? ) and in the condition of a ternary, an operand that carries an operator of its own is wrapped in parentheses. A simple operand — identifier, member access, call, template literal, unary negation — stays bare, and a chain of one logical operator is one expression. A ternary given whole — a value, an argument, a return — stays bare too: it is wrapped only as an operand of another operator. A Vue directive keeps its parentheses (VUE-06), and only a directive: a condition moved out of a v-if into a computed or a method loses them. return is_dev & 124;& 124; i === end - 1; ✗ no return is_dev & 124;& 124; (i === end - 1); ✓ yes return (!is_ready && !is_gone); ✗ no return !is_ready && !is_gone; ✓ yes (state === 'done') ? 'ok' : 'wait' url: (is_api ? '/api/v1' : null), ✗ no url: is_api ? '/api/v1' : null, ✓ yes A comparison beside // and a ternary condition, each wrapped in parentheses, and a ternary or a chain given whole, bare FORMATTING.md

items.name: One variable per declaration
items.text: Each variable gets its own const or let statement; a declaration never lists several variables separated by commas. The header of an indexed loop is the exception. const osc = c.createOscillator(), gain = c.createGain(); ✗ no const osc = c.createOscillator(); const gain = c.createGain(); ✓ yes One const declaring osc and gain, turned into a const for each FORMATTING.md

items.name: One blank line between top-level functions
items.text: Top-level functions stand one blank line apart: each function declared at module level is followed by one blank line before the next one. } function toggle_sound() ✗ no blank line } function toggle_sound() ✓ one blank line Two top-level functions with no blank line between them, turned into one blank line apart FORMATTING.md

items.name: Only the last argument spans lines
items.text: Only the last argument of a call may span several lines; nothing follows a multi-line argument — no further argument after } , no chained call after }) . A function that would leave arguments dangling is declared inside the caller and passed by name; a chained call becomes a variable. page.evaluate(function (text) { // ... }, text); ✗ dangling page.evaluate(find_families, text); ✓ yes items.filter(function (item) { // ... }).map(v = v.uid); ✗ dangling A call with an argument after its multi-line function, and a call chained after one, each rewritten so nothing dangles FORMATTING.md

items.name: Build strings with template literals
items.text: A string built from parts is a template literal; + never joins a string to a value. Plain quotes stay for a one-line string with nothing to interpolate; a string that spans lines is a template literal (SQL-01). 'weapons/turret-' + weapon.id ✗ no weapons/turret-${weapon.id} ✓ yes 'weapons/turret-' + weapon.id turned into a template literal FORMATTING.md

items.name: An empty function is {} on one line
items.text: An empty function expression or arrow is a no-op, as ignore is: its body is {} on one line, never split over two. A function declaration and a method keep their braces on lines of their own; a body holding only a comment is not empty. params.update = params.update function () { }; ✗ no params.update = params.update function () {}; ✓ yes promise.catch(() = {}); ✓ yes An empty function expression split over two lines, turned into {} on one line FORMATTING.md

items.name: let and const never share a run of declarations
items.text: A run of declarations, lines with no blank line between them, holds only let or only const . When a block needs both, they are two runs with one blank line between, the let run first, unless a let needs a value a const above it declares. That blank line is the one FMT-16 allows besides a phase change. const LIMIT = 10; let canvas = null; ✗ no const cache = new Map(); let canvas = null; ✓ yes const LIMIT = 10; const cache = new Map(); A let among the consts, turned into the let run, a blank line, then the const run FORMATTING.md

items.name: Prefer imperative control flow
items.text: A loop that keeps the uids of active items, beside its four steps in the order they run FORMATTING.md

items.name: No index needed: use for...of
items.text: Prefer for...of when the index is not needed. for (const item of items) { } An indexed loop that only fetches items(i), turned into for (const item of items) for_of.md

items.name: Use an indexed loop when the index is needed
items.text: for (let i = 0, end = items.length; i < end; ++i) { } Five items with their indexes: items(i) and items(i + 1) read together, so the loop counts for_of.md

items.name: No do...while
items.text: do { ... } while (...) does not exist. Use while or for . do...while with its condition at the bottom, turned into while with the condition first FORMATTING.md

items.name: Reduce and chains only on one line
items.text: reduce , deep chaining and functional pipelines are allowed only if the entire expression fits on a single line. A one-line reduce kept; a four-line filter, map and reduce chain turned into a loop FORMATTING.md

items.name: Arrows only for tiny callbacks
items.text: Do not use arrow functions for non-trivial logic. Arrows are allowed only for tiny callbacks. const uids = items.map(v = v.uid); fresh.catch(ignore); An arrow holding a conditional computation, turned into a named function; tiny arrows kept FORMATTING.md

items.name: A block-body arrow becomes a function
items.text: An arrow with a block body does not exist — it becomes function (...) {} , with an optional _this inside. The empty () = {} , a no-op, is the one exception (FMT-32). request.on('end', async () = { ✗ does not exist }); request.on('end', async function () { ✓ this }); An async arrow with a block body, turned into async function; the empty () = {} is the exception formatting_blocks.md

items.name: A catch that ignores the error binds nothing
items.text: try { } catch { } catch (error) with error never read, turned into catch {} formatting_blocks.md

items.name: Plain data: Set, Map or {}
items.text: Use plain data structures — Set , Map or plain {} for lookups. No prototypes, no mutation via shared state. A module may own its state, a singleton over its own data, written only by its own functions; shared means across modules, and that is what is forbidden. let modal = null; // the module's own function modal_show() { modal = modal_make(); } Set, Map and {} for lookups; another module writing modal state, turned into a module writing only its own FORMATTING.md

items.name: No implicit magic or hidden side effects
items.text: No implicit magic. No hidden side effects, no reliance on execution-order side effects. The one visible exception: side-effect imports, which sit at the very top of the file, in the order they run (FILE-11). import './sass/main.sass'; // the top of the file, in run order import './main-pre'; import Vue from 'vue'; A side-effect import hidden mid-list, moved to the top block in run order FORMATTING.md

items.name: A return-only callback is an arrow
items.text: Options-style methods retain function expressions (FMT-12). A callback whose body is only return , and whose arrow fits on one line, is written as that arrow — the mirror of FLOW-07. function stays for a callback that does more, or that needs this or arguments . items.filter(function (item) { return item_text(item) === text; }); ✗ no items.filter(v = item_text(v) === text); ✓ yes A filter callback that only returns, turned from a function into an arrow FORMATTING.md

items.name: Names are written whole
items.text: A constant, function, method, class or property is never glued together from strings at run time; a search or a rename must find it. A value that picks one of a few known names lists them with match (PHP) or switch (JavaScript). A name built at run time only for an open set that cannot be listed. constant(Invoice::class.'::STATUS_'.strtoupper($status)) ✗ no match ($status) { ✓ yes 'paid' = Invoice::STATUS_PAID, 'void' = Invoice::STATUS_VOID, } A search for STATUS_PAID misses a name glued at run time and finds it in a match that lists it whole names_written_whole.md

items.name: A library module exports one public value last
items.text: The value may be a function, class, configuration or data. Declare it above and export its name at file end; tool-shaped files follow their tool. module.exports = items_index_by_uid; A library file: requires, the value, helpers, and module.exports of that one value last FORMATTING.md

items.name: A script runs main and exports nothing
items.text: An executable script uses main as its entry function and does not export. A script that exports, turned into one that only runs: shebang, requires, cli(main), main FORMATTING.md

items.name: Library or executable, never both
items.text: Do not combine a library export and an executable invocation in the same file. A file that both exports and runs, split into a library and an executable FORMATTING.md

items.name: An executable hands main to cli
items.text: An executable hands its entry function to cli . cli owns the process contract: it keeps the event loop alive until main settles, reports a failure, and exits non-zero — ExitCodeError picks the code, any other error exits 1. A browser page script has no cli ; it calls main(); (MP-10). const cli = require('@vbarbarosh/node-helpers/src/cli'); cli(main); async function main() { } main handed to cli, which keeps the loop alive, reports a failure and exits non-zero cli_main.md

items.name: cli(main), never cli(main())
items.text: cli runs the function through Promise.try , so a synchronous throw is reported like a rejection; an already-invoked main() is a promise, and Promise.try rejects it with “expecting a function” — the app dies at startup. cli(main); ✓ right cli(main()); ✗ dies at startup cli(main()) hands cli a promise and dies at startup; cli(main) lets cli call main and report a throw cli_main.md

items.name: No hand-rolled catch and exit
items.text: A hand-rolled main().catch(...) with process.exit(1) does not exist. main().catch(function (error) { console.error(error); process.exit(1); }); ✗ does not exist A hand-written main().catch with process.exit(1), replaced by cli(main) cli_main.md

items.name: Nothing precedes the shebang
items.text: An executable script may start with a shebang; nothing may precede it. !/usr/bin/env node A comment above the shebang, moved below it so ! is line 1 FORMATTING.md

items.name: Imports sorted in byte order
items.text: The import block is sorted as plain text lines in byte order — what vim’s :sort over the block, or LC_ALL=C sort , produces. require and import alike. const $ = require('jquery'); const Vue = require('vue'); const axios = require('axios'); const cli = require('@vbarbarosh/node-helpers/src/cli'); const fs = require('fs'); const {promisify} = require('util'); Six requires in the order they were added, sorted in byte order as LC_ALL=C sort does FORMATTING.md

items.name: The whole line is the sort key
items.text: The whole line is the sort key — const or import included, not the module path and not the variable name. Requires sorted by name ignoring case, re-sorted by the whole line imports_sorted.md

items.name: Byte order, not locale order
items.text: Byte order, not locale order: @ and $ come before letters, uppercase before lowercase, and { after z — destructured imports land last. const Vue = require('vue'); ← V before a const axios = require('axios'); const {promisify} = require('util'); ← { after z Byte order: $ and @, then A to Z, a to z, then {; a locale-sorted list re-sorted that way imports_sorted.md

items.name: Imports form one unbroken list
items.text: The import block is one contiguous list: no groups for builtins, packages and local files, and no blank lines or comments inside it — either one breaks the sort. Two exceptions: a side-effect import keeps its run order in its own block at the top, and the named imports ( {foo, bar} ) may stand apart after the default ones — one blank line between blocks. import './sass/main.sass'; import './main-pre'; import Vue from 'vue'; import axios from 'axios'; import {mapState} from 'vuex'; import {promisify} from 'util'; Imports split by comments into groups, turned into one list with side-effect and named blocks imports_sorted.md

items.name: Constants follow the requires
items.text: File-level constants and variables follow the require statements. const REPORT_LIMIT = 31; A constant above the requires, moved below them FORMATTING.md

items.name: cli(main) right after initialization
items.text: cli(main); comes immediately after all global initialization, and no executable code other than that call may appear before the public entry function. Code run between cli(main) and main, turned into globals followed by cli(main) FORMATTING.md

items.name: The public entry function is the first function in the file
items.text: In an executable, the first function declaration is function main() . A helper above main, moved below so main is the first function FORMATTING.md

items.name: Helpers follow the entry function
items.text: Helpers are defined after the public entry function, and before a library’s final export. A library file: the entry function, its helpers, then the export FORMATTING.md

items.name: Helpers must be named functions, not inline lambdas
items.text: A helper written as an arrow in a constant, turned into a named function FORMATTING.md

items.name: This repository is CommonJS
items.text: This repository's own code and node scripts are CommonJS: const = require(''); , never import or export . Elsewhere the rules cover both module systems. import and export default, turned into require and module.exports in this repository FORMATTING.md

items.name: Libraries follow a fixed order
items.text: Library order is fixed. requires → constants → public entry → helpers → module.exports The five parts of a library in order: requires, constants, entry, helpers, exports FORMATTING.md

items.name: Executables follow a fixed order
items.text: Executable order is fixed. shebang → requires → globals → cli(main); → main() → helpers The six parts of a script in order: shebang, requires, globals, cli(main), main, helpers FORMATTING.md

items.name: One library export, last, and the file bears its name
items.text: A reusable/library module exports one public value; the file is named after that value. Declare it above and export its name last: module.exports = name; or export default name; . Never combine an ES-module declaration with its export or export an inline expression. Executable scripts export nothing; tool-shaped files follow the tool. The tool decides the export's shape, never the file's name (MP-53). // helper.js function helper() { return null; } export default helper; helper.js exporting a combined declaration or an inline expression, turned into helper declared, then exported by name one_export_per_file.md

items.name: No named exports; one public value per library module
items.text: Several independent public functions are several modules, each named after its export. One exported class can contain methods. Several names are never taken from a local module. export {engine_run, engine_transport}; ✗ no import {engine_run, engine_transport} from './engine'; ✗ no import engine_run from './engine_run'; ✓ yes import engine_transport from './engine_transport'; engine.js with two named exports, split into engine_run.js exporting one value one_export_per_file.md

items.name: Reusable scratch and test modules export one value too
items.text: Research, scratch and test-support modules are not exempt. Executable scripts export nothing; tool-shaped files follow the tool. A test fixtures module exporting two values, turned into users_fixture.js exporting one one_export_per_file.md

items.name: Libraries and tools dictate their own shape
items.text: A named import from a library is the library’s shape, and a file whose shape is dictated by a tool follows the tool — module.exports.mochaHooks in a mocha hooks file. import {mapState} from 'vuex'; vuex's named import and mocha's hooks file keep their tools' shape; a named import from a local module becomes one value one_export_per_file.md

items.name: New code takes its place from its surroundings where no explicit rule applies
items.text: Read the code around the insertion point — what stands together, in what order — and continue it within that scope. Explicit rules take priority (CORE-01); this does not require reorganizing existing code. format_time appended after render_page, moved beside the other format_ functions new_code_placement.md

items.name: A function family stays unbroken
items.text: A run of functions of one family — render_ , format_ , click_ — stays unbroken. A new member joins the run; a function of another family goes outside it, never between two members. render_css() describe() ✗ splits the run render_html() render_css() render_html() describe() ✓ after the run describe() between render_css and render_html, moved after the render run new_code_placement.md

items.name: One project shape; bin/ holds the verbs
items.text: Every project keeps one shape. A directory is a program, and bin/ holds its methods — one executable per verb, working the same in every language. bin/build bb bin/configure bin/release bin/run rr bin/self-check bin/test tt bin/watch ww The bin/ folder with build, configure, release, run, self-check, test and watch, and the same verbs in a node.js, a python and a php project layout.md

items.name: After git pull, run bin/configure
items.text: bin/configure is the only command to run after git pull to make a checkout ready for development. git pull, then bin/configure, then a checkout ready to work in; a list of remembered steps is replaced by that one command layout.md

items.name: Run, test, build and watch wrap npm
items.text: In a node.js project run , test , build and watch are usually thin wrappers over npm. The wrappers still earn their keep: rr , tt , bb , ww are shorter than any npm form, and the names hold for projects that are not node.js. alias rr='bin/run' alias tt='bin/test' alias bb='bin/build' alias ww='bin/watch' rr, tt, bb and ww call bin/run, bin/test, bin/build and bin/watch, which in a node.js project call npm start, npm test, npm run build and npm run watch layout.md

items.name: build/ is never committed; dist/ is the release
items.text: bin/build puts what it builds into build/ . build/ is temporary: it and everything in it are never committed. Taking something out of it into the repository is a decision of its own, as bin/release does with dist/ . dist/ holds the released build, committed by bin/release at release time only. There is one build: bin/release runs it and copies build/ into dist/ . build/ bin/build output, temporary, never committed dist/ released build, committed by bin/release bin/build writes build/, never committed; bin/release runs the build and copies build/ into dist/, committed at release time only layout.md

items.name: Runtime state in data/, never committed
items.text: data/ holds runtime state. Never committed. data/logs/2026-08-24.txt The running app writes data/logs/2026-08-24.txt; .gitignore lists data/, so git never sees it layout.md

items.name: .env belongs to whoever runs the app
items.text: .env is not the application's: docker loads it, or the Dockerfile sets the variables. The rules set nothing for it. docker loads .env, or the Dockerfile sets the variables, into the environment; the app only reads process.env layout.md

items.name: config/ turns the environment into configuration
items.text: config/ is the one place of the application's configuration. config/index.js reads the environment variables, may load files, and gives the code its configuration ready to use, through one path. // config/index.js module.exports = make_config(process.env); const config = require('../config'); process.env and files go into config/index.js, which gives the code one configuration object, read everywhere through require of config layout.md

items.name: src/ has a folder per part
items.text: src/ holds one subdirectory per part of the program. src/agent/ src/http/ src/android/ src/parser/ src/desktop-electron/ src/ holding one folder per part: agent, http, android, parser and desktop-electron layout.md

items.name: Shared helpers go to src/helpers/
items.text: Small shared functions go to src/helpers/ , one function per file. src/helpers/array_group.js src/helpers/ with array_group.js, array_index_by.js and string_slug.js, each holding the one function it is named after layout.md

items.name: A unit test sits next to the file it tests
items.text: src/helpers/array_group.js src/helpers/array_group.test.js array_group.test.js beside array_group.js in src/helpers/, instead of far away in tests/unit/ layout.md

items.name: tests/ drives the whole program
items.text: tests/ holds suites that drive the whole program, such as playwright. A playwright suite in tests/ drives a browser, which drives the whole running app layout.md

items.name: Keep the README short
items.text: README.md stays short: what the project is and how to start it. A short README with what the project is and how to start it; a long README of every detail is replaced by it and links to docs layout.md

items.name: Docs in docs/, notes in notes/, images in img/
items.text: docs/ holds the official documentation, notes/ holds working notes — hints and findings made during development — and img/ holds static images, mostly for the README. docs/ holds the official documentation, notes/ the working notes made during development, img/ the static images, mostly for the README layout.md

items.name: The project root carries the same standard files
items.text: .env is not one of them: it is there only when the runner puts it there (PROJ-06). .env.example .gitignore Dockerfile LICENSE README.md package.json The project root with .env.example, .gitignore, Dockerfile, LICENSE, README.md and package.json layout.md

items.name: A script starts from bin/templ
items.text: A new bash script is a copy of bin/templ with what it does not need thrown away. Its header, strict mode included, and the script / scriptdir / scriptname lines always stay; the colors, the exit message, the temporary directory with its EXIT trap and the four echo lines stay only if the script uses them. !/bin/bash http://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/bash.html The-Set-Builtin http://redsymbol.net/articles/unofficial-bash-strict-mode set -o nounset -o errexit -o pipefail script= realpath $0 scriptdir= dirname $script scriptname= basename $script bin/templ: the header and the script, scriptdir and scriptname lines always stay; the colors, the exit message, the temporary directory and the echo lines only if the script needs them templ

items.name: bin/configure asks everything up front
items.text: bin/configure asks every question it may have — the sudo password, a choice, a key — at the very start, before any work. Once the work has started there are no more questions; it never stops halfway, waiting for a password. Questions for a password, a choice and a key come first and the work runs to the end; a run that stops halfway to ask for a password is the wrong way configure.md

items.name: bin/configure takes sudo once, up front
items.text: bin/configure first works out what the run will need, predicting the state after the install. When a step will need sudo — an Electron chrome-sandbox that is missing, not root:4755 , or about to be replaced by the install — it takes sudo -v up front, and the later calls are sudo -n , which fail at once rather than prompt. sandbox=node_modules/electron/dist/chrome-sandbox state= stat -c %U:%a $sandbox 2 /dev/null wanted=… electron in package-lock.json installed=… electron in node_modules if & 91; "$wanted" != "$installed" ] & 91; "$state" != "root:4755" ]; then sudo -v fi sudo -n chown root:root $sandbox later: never a prompt bin/configure predicts the state after the install, takes sudo -v once if a step will need it, and later calls sudo -n, which never prompts configure.md

items.name: Everything kept lives in data/
items.text: data/ is the project's permanent data: a restart, a redeploy or a migration does not delete it. Everything the program writes and has to keep lives under data/ , and nowhere else. Configuration is not there: it comes from config/ and the environment. Uploads, the database and logs written by the program all live under data/, which survives restarts, redeploys and migrations; configuration comes from config/ and the environment data.md

items.name: Docker images carry code, not data
items.text: A docker image carries the code, never the data. One mount of data/ — a named volume or a host directory — is all it takes to keep it; moving the project is moving its data/ and running it with the same environment. docker run -v app-data:/app/data app docker run -v /srv/app/data:/app/data app An image with the code and a data/ volume mounted into the container; docker run -v app-data:/app/data app data.md

items.name: The README runs in a fixed order
items.text: A GitHub README.md runs in one order: badges, cover image, name, short description, website, quick start, documentation, license. Badges and the further documentation pages may be absent, and the website link is left out when the website is the documentation; the rest are always there. the parts of a README, top to bottom README.md

items.name: Badges at the top, a row per kind
items.text: Badges are optional. When there are any, they sit at the very top, above the cover, a row per kind: the package and its numbers on one row, the CI workflows on the next. As many as the project has. The top of a README: a row of package badges, a row of CI badges, then the cover image README.md

items.name: The cover image lives in img/
items.text: The cover image is a file in img/ , shown with and a dark twin when the colours need one.

items.name: The repository name is the one heading
items.text: The name is the one heading, right under the cover: the name of the repository. rules A README with the cover, then rules as its one level-one heading, then sections README.md

items.name: One description sentence everywhere
items.text: The short description is one sentence on its own line, and the same sentence is the repository's About text and the description of package.json . One sentence, written once, appears as the README description, the GitHub About text and the description of package.json README.md

items.name: A link with the text Website follows the description
items.text: Its address is the repository's About → Website and the homepage of package.json . It is left out when the website is the documentation. Website A Website link under the description, with the same address as the GitHub About website and the homepage field of package.json README.md

items.name: A quick start in a few lines
items.text: A quick start shows how to install and run the project, in a few lines. npx vbarbarosh/rules src A quick start of one line, npx vbarbarosh/rules src, that installs and runs the project README.md

items.name: Documentation opens with the full docs link
items.text: A Documentation section opens with the link to the full documentation. Further pages follow as a short list, each with what it covers. Documentation Full documentation: & 42;& 42;& 91;docs/rules.html](docs/rules.html)& 42;& 42; & 42; & 91;Formatting](FORMATTING.md) — the JavaScript spec A Documentation section: the full documentation link first, then a short list of further pages with what each covers README.md

items.name: License is the last section
items.text: License is the last section: the license named and linked to LICENSE . License & 91;MIT](LICENSE) The README sections in order with License last, linking to the LICENSE file README.md

items.name: Demos live in demos/
items.text: Small demos — a short runnable file that shows how something is used — live in demos/ , never in examples/ . demos/items_by.js ✓ right examples/items_by.js ✗ wrong examples/items_by.js is wrong; the same demo lives in demos/items_by.js layout.md

items.name: The build ends with the self-check
items.text: The last step of bin/build runs bin/self-check : the application's own check that it is fit to work, one probe per thing it needs, the programs it calls and what the build was to produce; a lit lamp names what to fix (TEST-09). A build that fails it ships nothing. bin/build, the last step bin/self-check [ffmpeg] ffmpeg version 6.1.1 [pyftsubset] zopfli: 4120 < 5312 bytes build/front.d: missing ✗ ships nothing bin/build ends with bin/self-check, whose probes find ffmpeg and pyftsubset but a missing build/front.d, so the build ships nothing layout.md

items.name: A project can ship a prebuilt dist/
items.text: A project can distribute a prebuilt dist/ from the repository, the way Vue, VueRouter, Vuex, jQuery, Bootstrap, Axios, Cuid and Jsondiffpatch do. dist/vue.js in the repository, served by unpkg, loaded by a page with a script tag, with no build on the user side packaging.md

items.name: Release order: clean, bump, build, commit, tag
items.text: The release workflow is fixed: ensure there are no changes, increase the version, update dist/ , commit, tag. dist/ is updated by the one build, then a copy of build/ (MP-32). test -z "$(git status --porcelain)" npm version $1 --no-git-tag-version rm -rf build npm run build rm -rf dist cp -r build dist git add package.json package-lock.json dist git commit -m "release: v$(...)" git tag v$(...) A release in five steps: no changes, bump the version, build and copy build/ into dist/, commit, tag packaging.md

items.name: The script commits and tags, not the bump
items.text: Bump the version without committing or tagging, then own both steps in the script. npm version $1 --no-git-tag-version npm version without its git tag bumps the version only; the release script then commits and tags packaging.md

items.name: One command does the whole release
