items.name: A commit title is a scope, a colon and a short description
items.text: The scope is one or two words: the part of the project the commit changes, its category. maps: placement rules for gates and portals, and map-check The title maps: placement rules for gates and portals, and map-check, as a scope, a colon and a description commits.md

items.name: Commit titles are lowercase
items.text: The title is all lowercase, names included. readme: elites and arcade saves as the code has them ✓ yes README: Elites and arcade saves ✗ no README: Elites and arcade saves is wrong; readme: elites and arcade saves as the code has them is right commits.md

items.name: A commit title is 72 characters at most
items.text: The whole title, scope included, stays within 72 characters. Short is the rule; 72 is the ceiling, not a target. maps: one name for the gate jump reach 38 docs: build-docs and a github pages workflow 44 72 at most Title lengths as bars against a line at 72 characters: 38 and 44 fit, 89 runs past it; the long one is cut to fit commits.md

items.name: A short body, only when needed
items.text: Details go in a body after one blank line, only when they are really needed. A body is short, in ordinary sentences. docs: link the placement rules, gates and portals as they stand docs/README.md lists placement.md; objects.md describes gates and portals as the placement rules now put them. A commit with a title, a blank line and a two-line body, beside a commit that needs no body commits.md

items.name: A body wraps at 72 characters
items.text: Every line of the body stays within 72 characters, as the title does, and breaks between words. A path, a URL or a command longer than that keeps a line of its own, whole. docs: the agents page has a picture for each guide Consequences first: the task, its four what-if questions and what each shapes. One example, all cases: only the shown dropdown fixed against every case found. A commit body wrapped at 72 characters, each line ending before a red line at column 72 commits.md

items.name: One line, one event, four fields
items.text: A log is one stream of lines, as if one infinite file; its files may be split by day (PROJ-05). One physical line records one event, in four fields and nothing else. [time][group_uid][sender] details A log line as its four fields, time, group_uid, sender and details, each with what it holds, above three such lines of one log logs.md

items.name: Measurements go in details
items.text: Elapsed time, status and every other measurement belong in details , not in a field of their own. [cd8e5vqp][db_query_end_error] 30.001s ETIMEDOUT The fields of a line with the measurements in details; a fifth bracketed field for 30.001s beside the same line with it in details logs.md

items.name: time is ISO-8601 UTC with milliseconds
items.text: 2026-08-17T16:09:20.185Z An ISO-8601 UTC time split into date, T, time, milliseconds and Z; a local time and an epoch each beside the ISO form logs.md

items.name: Omit time when the runtime stamps it
items.text: Include time when writing directly to a file; omit it when the runtime already timestamps the line, as docker does. & 91;2026-08-17T16:09:20.185Z]& 91;cd8e5vqp]& 91;db_query_begin] name=select_users & 91;cd8e5vqp]& 91;db_query_begin] name=select_users A line written to a file carries its time; under docker, docker's timestamp stands before the app's line, and a doubled time beside the line written once logs.md

items.name: Every event carries its group uid
items.text: A group is one unit of work — a request, a job, a cron run. Every event carries its group’s uid, an opaque string, usually a cuid. Four lines of one request, each starting with its group uid cd8e5vqp; a line without a uid beside the same line with it logs.md

items.name: A group opens with group_spawn
items.text: The first event of a group is group_spawn , emitted synchronously before the uid is passed to other work or another event is emitted for the group. A root group omits parent= . & 91;new_group_uid]& 91;group_spawn] parent=old_group_uid & 91;c1a0root]& 91;group_spawn] A child group and a root group, each opening with group_spawn; a spawn after the first work beside the spawn first logs.md

items.name: The caller's uid becomes the parent
items.text: Messages and requests carry the caller’s uid; the receiver uses it as the parent of its new group. A web group sends a job, the message carries its uid, and the worker's group_spawn names it as parent; a spawn without parent beside one with parent=aaa logs.md

items.name: A sender names one call site
items.text: sender identifies one logging call site, and the name is unique in the whole codebase — a grep for it lands on one place. Think of it as a const in a single namespace. A grep for a sender lands on one line of code; one sender in two places beside a name for each place logs.md

items.name: sender is snake_case
items.text: ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_] $ The snake_case pattern of a sender; camelCase and hyphenated senders each beside db_query_begin logs.md

items.name: Every begin is closed by its end
items.text: A _begin event is closed by the same stem with _end_ok or _end_error , in the same group. An end never appears without its begin in that group. & 91;c9k2vf3p]& 91;group_spawn] & 91;c9k2vf3p]& 91;mp4gif_worker_begin] & 91;c9k2vf3p]& 91;mp4gif_worker_end_ok] 4.512s & 91;c7t0xb1m]& 91;group_spawn] & 91;c7t0xb1m]& 91;mp4gif_worker_begin] & 91;c7t0xb1m]& 91;mp4gif_worker_end_error] 0.884s ffmpeg exit=1 A begin closed by end_ok and a begin closed by end_error; an end with no begin beside the begin and its end logs.md

items.name: A plain end when the outcome speaks
items.text: Use _end when the logged outcome — an HTTP status, say — already says what happened and classifying it as ok or error would mislead. An HTTP request closed by a plain end with its 404; an end_error for the 404 beside the plain end logs.md

items.name: Spawn a group only when it pays
items.text: A group costs at least three lines. Spawn one only when the work earns them: seconds of work, or many logging call sites. Do not spawn a group for one short call. & 91;bbb]& 91;group_spawn] parent=aaa & 91;bbb]& 91;process_begin] & 91;bbb]& 91;process_end_ok] 0.000s ✗ noise Three lines of a group spawned for one short call beside the two lines on the caller's group; a group earns its lines with seconds of work or many call sites logs.md

items.name: Log short work on the caller’s group, not a new one
items.text: When nothing is reported between the two ends, record one event. & 91;aaa]& 91;process_begin] & 91;aaa]& 91;process_end_ok] 0.000s & 91;aaa]& 91;process_handled] 0.000s ✓ even better A group spawned for nothing beside the begin and end on the caller's group, and one process_handled line, even better logs.md

items.name: No lone end in a new group
items.text: Two lines are the same noise when a new group holds a lone end. The matching begin was emitted on the parent — keep the pair there. & 91;bbb]& 91;group_spawn] parent=aaa & 91;bbb]& 91;process_end_ok] 0.000s ✗ noise An end that strayed into a new group beside the begin and end together on the parent logs.md

items.name: Details are terse, on one line
items.text: details are human-readable and terse, and never contain a physical newline. A details with a newline, its second line without fields, beside the same event on one terse line logs.md

items.name: No secrets or payloads in details
items.text: details never contain secrets, tokens, signed URLs, URL query values, bodies or headers. Prefer a reference to the payload over the payload. A token, a signed URL and a body each beside a reference that replaces it: a user uid, a file path, a size logs.md

items.name: Simple words bare, the rest JSON-quoted
items.text: A printable ASCII word without spaces, double quotes, backslashes or square brackets is written bare — exactly the bytes that were sent, so it cannot span words, break the line, or mint a fake tag. Every other string is JSON-quoted. name=select_users reason="db timeout" value="" A bare word and two JSON-quoted values with why; an unquoted value with a space and a bracketed value each beside its quoted form logs.md

items.name: Structures as compact JSON
items.text: Arrays, objects, booleans and null use compact JSON. retry=true limits={"soft":10,"hard":25} retry and limits as compact JSON; spaced JSON and a yes for a boolean each beside the compact form logs.md

items.name: An unordered list is sorted and prefixed with its count
items.text: Ordered values are not sorted. 3:& 91;180,783,846] 2:& 91;"bar","foo"] 0:& 91;] Three lists turned into their sorted, counted form; a list in order of arrival beside 3:(180,783,846) logs.md

items.name: Truncate on UTF-8, count what is cut
items.text: Truncation preserves valid UTF-8 and ends with the number of omitted bytes. ...+4821 A long value cut and 4 821 bytes counted; a cut inside a character beside a whole one ending ...+4821 logs.md

items.name: Try to keep one log line under 2k UTF-8 bytes
items.text: A log line describes an event; it is not payload storage. A 120-byte event under the 2 KB mark and a 48 000-byte payload far past it; the payload beside a counted, truncated line logs.md

items.name: group_exit is optional; nothing follows it
items.text: group_exit is optional and mainly serves to detect leaks. After it is emitted, no producer emits another event for that group; a parent may emit it for work it abandons. Consumers must accept groups without it — its absence makes no claim. [group_uid][group_exit] A group closed by group_exit and a note that it is optional; an event after the exit beside the exit last logs.md

items.name: After means emission order, not timestamps
items.text: “After” group_exit means producer emission order, not timestamp or collector ingestion order. Buffering may deliver an older event later; that alone is not an error. Without a causal-order signal — preserved per-group order, a shared sequence — cross-process detection is advisory. Two events emitted in one order and received in the other; judging by arrival beside judging by emission logs.md

items.name: Utilities first, app classes next, local classes last
items.text: Classes inside one class="…" attribute keep a fixed order. Plain utilities lead; an app-prefixed class ( vb- , np- — one prefix per app, app- in these examples) sorts after all of them, base class included; a file-local - class is always last. layout spacing sizing decoration typography app-prefix local <div class="flex-row-c -root" / <div class="fluid p30 xpt app-scrollbars-light -grid" / <div class="db w80 h80 br4 fit-cover cur-pointer app-background -preset-img" / <div class="flex-row-cl gap10 app-font-b14 -title-trigger" / The class order as chips, from layout to local, and an example class list labelled by family; local first beside utilities, app, local css_classes.md

items.name: Item class leads; gap closes the layout
items.text: Within the utilities: an item class ( fluid , grow , shrink , flex-fluid , flex-grow , flex-nogrow , flex-shrink , flex-noshrink , flex-static ) or a display or position utility ( db , abs ) leads where the element carries one; a gap closes the layout group — every flex , grid or split class first, then the gap; grid and flex never share an element; ph precedes pv , and spacing comes before typography. fluid flex-row gap10 oa flex-row flex-align-center gap10 mt10 flex-col-c gap15 grid-foo gap5 fluid flex-row gap10 oa and flex-row flex-align-center gap10 mt10 as labelled chips; gap first and flex with grid each beside its right order css_classes.md

items.name: No class without a rule
items.text: Every class either has a rule in the file’s own style block or is an established project utility. An element that needs no styling stays classless — a label-only class rots and sends the next reader looking for a rule nobody wrote. <!-- the wrapper is not styled, so it carries no class -- <div <div class=" -funnel-bars" ...</div </div A wrapper div without a class around a styled -funnel-bars and its rule; a -wrapper with no rule beside the classless wrapper css_classes.md

items.name: Gap for flex and grid, mg and mi for blocks
items.text: gap spaces the children of a grid or flex container; mg and mi are the block-container forms. The two do not mix. A flex row spaced by gap10 and a block spaced by mg10; mg10 on a flex row beside gap10 css_classes.md

items.name: Fluid in a split, flex-fluid in a flex
items.text: fluid marks the filling child of an hsplit / vsplit (whose children default to flex: none ); flex-fluid marks the growing child of a plain flex-row / flex-col . Same CSS — the choice states which container the element sits in. A fluid child filling an hsplit and a flex-fluid child growing in a flex-row; flex-fluid in a split beside fluid css_classes.md

items.name: Broad before narrow
items.text: An x class usually comes before the setter it clears the way for — the broad class leads and the narrow one corrects it, whichever of the two is the reset. <div class="xm ml5" / <!-- margin: 0; margin-left: 5px; -- <div class="m5 xml" / <!-- margin: 5px; margin-left: 0; -- xm ml5 and m5 xml with the margins each produces; the reset after the setter beside the reset first css_classes.md

items.name: Rows and columns are a table
items.text: Rows and columns are a , not a stack of flex rows — the columns line up only until one cell is wider. Flex rows stay for content that is genuinely not tabular. A stack of flex rows whose columns drift beside a table whose columns line up, and their code css_classes.md

items.name: Imports and includes come first
items.text: @import comes first in a block; @include comes first in a rule, ahead of the property declarations — the mixin brings the base, the block overrides it. . -card @include app-transition(box-shadow, border-color) box-sizing: border-box A rule with the include after a declaration beside the same rule with the include first css_classes.md

items.name: Transitions come from the mixin
items.text: A transition: property is not written by hand — @include app-transition(props…) fills it, expanding each property into at the shared default speed. app-transition-fast and app-transition-debug are the same mixin at the shared fast and debug speeds. List the exact properties that change, never all , and put the include on the base rule rather than the state variant, so the animation covers both directions. The mixin is Sass; plain .css files are not checked for it. @include app-transition(box-shadow, border-color) The transition mixin expanding into each property at the shared speed; transition: all by hand beside the mixin with exact properties css_classes.md

items.name: Five families: layout, spacing, sizing, decoration, typography
items.text: What each family holds: layout is the flex/grid/split container and its flex- modifiers; spacing is p / m ; sizing is w / h / max-w / min-h ; decoration is br , fit-cover , cur-pointer and the other shape and surface utilities; typography is fs fw lh , then alignment and nowrap . The five families, layout, spacing, sizing, decoration and typography, with examples; a mixed-up class list beside the family order css_classes.md

items.name: A header aligns like its column
items.text: A table header is aligned the way its column's data is: centered data, centered header; right-aligned data, right-aligned header. A table with a centered header over right-aligned numbers beside one whose header aligns as its column css_classes.md

items.name: One selector per line
items.text: A selector list puts each selector on its own line, the comma closing the line; the brace follows the last one. .docs th, .docs td { ✗ no .docs th, .docs td { ✓ yes Two selectors on one line beside one selector a line, the comma closing each css_classes.md

items.name: One blank line between rules
items.text: Rules stand one blank line apart: each closing brace is followed by one empty line before the next selector — never two, never none. .hidden { display: none !important; } .intro { ✗ no blank line .hidden { display: none !important; } .intro { ✓ one blank line Two rules with no blank line between them beside the same rules one blank line apart css_classes.md

items.name: A long query opens and closes on its own line
items.text: A query that spans lines opens its template literal with a line break and closes it on a line of its own; the query is indented one level deeper than the call that runs it. await knex.raw( UPDATE user_identities ... ); A query glued to its knex.raw call beside the query opening and closing on its own lines, indented one level sql.md

items.name: Keywords upper case, names lower case
items.text: Every keyword, type and function is upper case; tables, columns, indexes and aliases stay lower case, spelled as the schema spells them. SELECT MIN(id) AS id FROM user_identities ✓ yes select min(id) as id from user_identities ✗ no A query's tokens as keywords and names; an all-lower-case query beside keywords upper case and names lower case sql.md

items.name: Each clause on its own line
items.text: The dialect is MySQL. At the top level of a statement, each clause starts a line of its own — SELECT , FROM , every JOIN , UPDATE , SET , CREATE UNIQUE INDEX , ON , WHERE , ALTER TABLE , DROP INDEX — and what the clause takes goes on the next line, indented four spaces. A keyword of several words stays on one line. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX user_identities_primary_user_id_unique ON user_identities (primary_user_id) DROP INDEX user_identities_primary_user_id_unique ON user_identities A CREATE UNIQUE INDEX whose clauses run on beside each clause on its line with its operand indented under it sql.md

items.name: A subquery body is indented between its parentheses
items.text: A subquery opens with ( at the end of the line that uses it; its body is indented one level, and ) closes it on a line of its own at that line's indent, followed by the alias. WHERE id IN ( SELECT id FROM ( SELECT MIN(id) AS id ... ) AS oldest ) A flat nested subquery beside the same subquery indented a level per pair of parentheses sql.md

items.name: Short expressions may stay on one line
items.text: A short expression can stay on one line: a WHERE that opens a subquery, even at the top level, and the clauses inside a subquery. WHERE id IN ( SELECT id FROM ( SELECT MIN(id) AS id FROM user_identities A WHERE split to the word beside short expressions kept on one line inside the subquery sql.md

items.name: One ALTER TABLE action per clause
items.text: Each action of an ALTER TABLE is a clause of its own, its operand indented under it; the comma between two actions ends the first operand's line. A column definition stays whole on its line. ALTER TABLE user_identities DROP INDEX user_identities_primary_user_id_unique, DROP COLUMN primary_user_id An ALTER TABLE with its actions run together beside one action per clause, each operand indented sql.md

items.name: Every component is provided with three global methods through a mixin
items.text: px(value) // format a pixel value uid(& 91;name]) // ids unique across components emit_input(value) // return a value from an input One globals mixin hands px, uid and emit_input to every component vue-globals.md

items.name: Ids come from uid
items.text: Generated ids are bound to the current element and are what id and label[for] use. The name uid was chosen so it does not conflict with the id attribute every element may carry. uid: function (name) { return name ? c${this.& 95;uid}& 95;${name} : c${this.& 95;uid} ; }, The component's _uid 42 and uid('email') make the id c42_email, used by both the label and the input vue-globals.md

items.name: Spell out v-on and v-bind
items.text: The shorthands @ and : are not used. The shorthands :src and @click beside the same element written with v-bind:src and v-on:click vue-formatting.md

items.name: Attributes keep one order
items.text: ref v-if v-for v-on v-bind:ref v-bind [...] class type placeholder title The ten attributes in their order, ref first and title last, and an input element written in that order vue-formatting.md

items.name: Lift v-if off a v-for
items.text: Avoid v-if and v-for on the same component — lift the condition to a . <template v-if="items" <div v-for="item in items" v-bind:key="item.uid" {{ item.title }} </div </template A div carrying both v-for and v-if beside the condition lifted to a template around the loop vue-formatting.md

items.name: Compound directive values in parentheses
items.text: A simple directive value stays bare; a compound one is wrapped in parentheses. Every directive — v-if , v-else-if , v-show , v-on , v-bind . Simple is a single identifier, member access, method call, template literal or unary negation; compound is anything carrying a binary operator or a ternary. Only in a template: inside an attribute's quotes a compound value is easy to miss, and the parentheses show it. The same value moved into script, a computed or a method, loses them and follows FMT-27. <template v-if="is_ready" <template v-if="(is_loading_fonts & 124;& 124; is_loading_images)" <div v-bind:class="(compact ? 'narrow' : 'wide')" / An operator and a ternary left bare beside the same values in parentheses, and a simple value wrapped beside it bare vue-formatting.md

items.name: An input works like a native input
items.text: Anything which takes data from a user is called an input and must work as a normal INPUT element. 1. takes data from the value property 2. emits an input event 3. respects the disabled state 4. respects the readonly attribute 5. reacts to clicks on the associated LABEL 6. reacts to mouse hover from that LABEL 7. injects and uses app_form_input_id 8. takes focus with the TAB key app-input-email takes value, disabled and readonly, emits input, and answers a click on its label and the Tab key like an input vue-input.md

items.name: Avoid generic inputs
items.text: Avoid generic inputs — those with a lot of properties like min , max , step . One app-input-number with min, max, step and more beside app-input-percent, app-input-px and app-input-year vue-input.md

items.name: Forms submit by button and Enter
items.text: Compose forms from app-form-div and app-label , inside a whose submit the submit button and the Enter key both reach. <form v-on:submit.prevent="submit" class="mg10" <app-form-div class="flex-row gap10" <app-label Email:</app-label <app-input-email v-model="user.email" / </app-form-div </form A form whose field (Enter) and Submit button both reach its one submit handler vue-form.md

items.name: Cancel and submit close the form
items.text: A form’s buttons close the form: cancel returns false through vue-modal’s modal.return , submit is a type="submit" button. <app-button-orange v-on:click="modal.return(false)" Cancel </app-button-orange <app-button-green type="submit" Submit </app-button-green A Rename file form: Cancel returns false through modal.return and closes; Submit is a type submit button that saves and closes vue-form.md

items.name: One button, one class
items.text: A button assembled from btn btn-green btn-lg beside one class, button-green vue-button.md

items.name: A slider thumb moves from 0 to 100%
items.text: A slider is usually a container and a thumb. Prefer positioning the thumb with top or left from 0 to 100% — 0 means empty, 100% means full. left: 0 // empty left: 100% // full Three sliders with the thumb at left 0, 50% and 100%: empty, half and full vue-slider.md

items.name: One SVG icon per file
items.text: Each SVG icon goes into its own svg-icon- .vue file, containing only a TEMPLATE element with an SVG inside. <template <svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" xmlns="http& 58;//www& 46;w3.org/2000/svg" <path fill="currentColor" d="..." / </svg </template A folder of svg-icon- .vue files and the one file content: a template with an SVG whose path fills currentColor vue-svg-icon.md

items.name: Icons use currentColor
items.text: SVG icons respect the currentColor CSS property. The same archive icon in a plain, an accent and a danger button, taking each button text colour vue-svg-icon.md

items.name: Component options keep one order
items.text: props inject provide mixins data computed watch methods mounted created beforeDestroy The eleven component options in their order, from props to beforeDestroy vue-components.md

items.name: Name a handler by event and button text
items.text: An event handler is named after the UI part it is bound to — the event, then the button text. <button v-on:click="click_approve" Approve </button The Approve button handled by click_approve; handle_click beside it, saying nothing of the button vue-components.md

items.name: A handler on an icon is named after the icon
items.text: <button v-on:click="click_icon_archive" <svg-icon-archive / </button An archive icon button handled by click_icon_archive; click_button beside it, naming no button vue-components.md

items.name: Rename the handler with its label
items.text: After the text or icon is changed, rename the corresponding event handler. Approve → Accept // click_approve → click_accept Approve with click_approve; after the label becomes Accept, click_approve left stale beside click_accept vue-components.md

items.name: Empty elements close themselves
items.text: An element without a body closes itself — a component, an HTML element and a void element alike. This holds in .vue files and string templates; an in-DOM template is parsed by the browser first. <th </th ✗ no <th / ✓ yes <app-input-email v-model="user.email" / An empty th, an empty component and a bare br left open, each beside its self-closing form vue-formatting.md

items.name: A piece shown in two places is a component
items.text: Whatever the screen shows in more than one place, a badge most often, is a Vue component of its own, used in each place. Never the same markup and classes copied: a change then reaches some copies and misses the others. <span class="flex-row-cl gap5 br999 -reply" ✗ no In progress {{ detail }} </span <badge-in-progress v-bind:detail="detail" / ✓ yes One badge-in-progress component used in the list and in the detail, beside markup copied into each place vue-components.md

items.name: Named kind first
items.text: A component is named - , as icons are svg-icon- . Sorted by name, every component of a kind sits together. badge-filing badge-in-progress badge-no-reply Components named what-kind scatter when sorted; named kind-what, each kind sorts together vue-components.md

items.name: What changes is a prop
items.text: What differs from place to place goes in as a prop: a count, a time, a plan's progress. The component holds the rest. <badge-new v-bind:count="3" / // 3 new <badge-in-progress detail="for 4 h" / badge-new with count 3 and 12 and badge-in-progress with a detail, each rendering its own badge vue-components.md

items.name: A variant is a suffix
items.text: A smaller or otherwise different form is a component of its own, named with a suffix; never a second copy written by hand where it is needed. badge-in-progress → badge-in-progress-sm badge-in-progress and its smaller badge-in-progress-sm; a badge shrunk by a class at one place beside the variant vue-components.md

items.name: A kind shares one look through one mixin
items.text: What every component of a kind shares, its shape, size and type, comes from one Sass mixin; each component sets only its own colours. . -root @include app-badge background: var(--accent-soft) color: var(--accent) The app-badge mixin gives shape, size and type to badge-new, badge-done and badge-waiting, each with its own colours vue-components.md

items.name: Every screen has a light/dark switch
items.text: An app screen, a report, a standalone page: each shows a switch the reader can click. Following the OS setting alone does not count. One exception: a page made only to be photographed for a rule's picture keeps no switch. An app screen, a report and a standalone page, each with a theme switch; following the OS setting alone beside a switch on every screen theme_switch.md

items.name: Two states, one shared icon button
items.text: Show the current theme: sun for Light, crescent for Dark. Use img/theme-sun.svg and img/theme-moon.svg ; size and border may vary. Click toggles directly, with no menu, System or Auto option. Sun: Light → Crescent: Dark → Sun: Light One button cycling sun, crescent, sun with each click; a Light, Dark, System menu beside it theme_switch.md

items.name: The dark theme redefines the light colors

items.name: Use optimistic updates; the user keeps working
items.text: Keep the backend snapshot immutable and local pending changes separate. Show the local change and send its update immediately. After acknowledgement, reread the backend, replace the snapshot, and clear only the pending change confirmed by that result; preserve later actions and reject stale refreshes. Show the change where the user made it, at once, marked as waiting, whatever route it takes inside. Keep failures visible as unsynchronized and retry safely; if only the reread failed, retry that step. Read → local overlay → update → acknowledgement → refresh → replace snapshot → clear confirmed overlay Send is pressed: on the left the comment is nowhere for 2 seconds, then it shows; on the right it shows at once marked Sending, and the mark goes when the server has it optimistic_updates.md

items.name: A document has two halves
items.text: The author writes the top half, compressed around what he already knows; the AI writes the bottom half, restating it for a reader who lacks that context. A document as two stacked halves: the author's compressed notes on top, the AI's restated explanation below, each written by one of them WRITING.md

items.name: Author sources govern the explanation
items.text: Read the top half and applicable manually approved rules. An approved entry may explicitly clarify older wording within its scope; if the sources disagree without such a decision, ask before regenerating. The author's half and the approved rules feed the AI, which writes the explanation; when they disagree with no approved entry, the AI asks first WRITING.md

items.name: No AI patches the top half
items.text: The one exception is an explicit request from the author. An AI rewording of the author's line, wrong, beside the line kept word for word; the one exception is the author asking for it WRITING.md

items.name: Regenerate the bottom half from both sources, never edit it
items.text: After the top half or an applicable manually approved rule changes, regenerate the explanation from both. Preserve approved decisions and their scope. A change on top leads to the whole bottom half written again from both sources; patching one line of the bottom is wrong WRITING.md

items.name: Usually a heading starts the bottom half
items.text: Most of the time the bottom half starts with a heading, and that heading is the boundary. A --- line or a closing fence before it is decoration. There is no strict marker. --- ✨ AI-Generated Content Below ✨ --- The author's notes, a decorative --- line, then the heading that is the real boundary of the AI's half WRITING.md

items.name: Tiny arrows fit one line
items.text: A tiny arrow is a single-line expression callback or value factory, passed as a call argument or as an object property value; an empty () = {} is one too (FMT-32). items.name: agent
items.text: harness + model + tools + policy. Never the model alone. Agent: harness, model, tools and policy in one box, the workspace beside it agents.md

items.name: model
items.text: The LLM, identified by a string ( claude-opus-5 ). Stateless: one context in, one message out. Model: a context in, one message out, nothing remembered between calls agents.md

items.name: harness
items.text: The code that runs the loop: builds context, calls the model, executes tools, appends results, stops. Harness: the loop of building the context, calling the model, running the tools, appending, stopping agents.md

items.name: tool
items.text: A named operation the model may request. The model sees its definition; the harness owns its implementation. Tool: the definition the model sees, the implementation the harness owns agents.md

items.name: policy
items.text: Text in the system message that constrains behavior. Read, not enforced. Enforcement is permission, gate and sandbox. Policy: text the model reads; what must not happen is stopped by permission, gate and sandbox agents.md

items.name: skill
items.text: Instructions loaded into context on demand, not resident in every call. Skill: instructions on a shelf, loaded into the context only when asked for agents.md

items.name: workspace
items.text: What tools act on: a repo, a canvas, an app database. Workspace: a repository, a canvas or an app database, what the tools act on agents.md

items.name: user
items.text: Who starts a turn: a person or a calling application. User: a person or an application starts a turn agents.md

items.name: operator
items.text: Who configures and deploys the agent. Operator: writes the policy, picks the model and tools, sets limits, deploys agents.md

items.name: call
items.text: One request to the model. Call: one request to the model, inside a round, a turn, a session, a run agents.md

items.name: round
items.text: One call plus execution of the tool_calls it returned. Zero tool_calls for a final. Round: one call plus the tool_calls it returned agents.md

items.name: turn
items.text: One user message (or one scheduled task) through to the final. One or many rounds. One user message, or one scheduled task, through to its last final: one round or many. The checks after a final belong to the same turn: when the tests fail, the harness sends the failure back and the fixing goes on in the same turn, so max_rounds and the budget cover it too (MP-60). Turn: one user message through to the final, one or many rounds agents.md

items.name: session
items.text: Ordered turns sharing one transcript. Session: ordered turns sharing one transcript agents.md

items.name: run
items.text: One launch of the harness process (CLI invocation, cron job). Run: one launch of the harness, holding the session agents.md

items.name: message
items.text: One unit of the transcript. Has a role: system, user, assistant, tool. Message: one unit of the transcript with its role agents.md

items.name: transcript
items.text: Every message of the session so far, append-only. Includes tool_calls and tool_results. Transcript: every message so far, append-only agents.md

items.name: context
items.text: What one call sends: system, tool_definitions, the transcript or its compacted form, grounding. What surrounds a thing and gives it its meaning: the sentence around a word, the conversation around a message, the project around a file. The same words mean different things in different contexts, so the context is read first and the thing after. For an AI model, the context is the context window: everything it reads before it answers, counted in tokens. One call sends it whole: the system message, the tool definitions, the transcript or its compacted form, the grounding. The model has nothing else: what is not in the context does not exist for it, and what falls out of it (compacted away, or left behind when a session ends) is gone unless it was written down somewhere it will be read again, a note, a file, a database. Context: system message, tool definitions, the transcript or its summary, grounding, sent whole to the model agents.md

items.name: sidecar
items.text: A second payload carried beside a message, never merged into it: the untruncated tool output, file handles, timings. The request goes over the wire; the sidecar stays with the harness. Sidecar: the small message over the wire, the large payload kept by the harness agents.md

items.name: memory
items.text: What outlives one context: the transcript, plus external stores (notes, a database). Memory: the transcript, notes, files and databases that outlive one context agents.md

items.name: system
items.text: The message that holds the policy. Tool_definitions travel beside it, not in it. System: the message holding the policy, the tool definitions beside it agents.md

items.name: tool_call
items.text: Model → harness: tool name, arguments, id. Tool call: name, arguments and id, from the model to the harness agents.md

items.name: tool_result
items.text: Harness → model: output or error of one tool_call, paired by id. Data, never instructions. Tool result: output or error back to the model, paired by id, data not instructions agents.md

items.name: final
items.text: An assistant message with no tool_call. Ends the turn. Says nothing about whether the task succeeded. An assistant message with no tool_call. It ends the turn once the checks after it pass; when a check fails, the failure goes back and another final comes later in the same turn. A final says nothing about whether the task succeeded. final is our name, not an API's (MP-60). Final: an assistant message with no tool_call ends the turn; its claim still needs a check agents.md

items.name: stop_reason
items.text: Why a call ended: final, tool_call, max_tokens, refusal. The names are the API's. Why a call ended: final, tool_call, max_tokens, refusal. These are our own names; each API spells them its way. Anthropic's stop_reason says end_turn for a final, tool_use for a tool_call, max_tokens and refusal ; OpenAI's finish_reason says stop , tool_calls , length and content_filter (MP-60). Stop reason: final, tool_call, max_tokens or refusal agents.md

items.name: readonly

items.name: mutating

items.name: destructive

items.name: permission
items.text: What the harness lets a tool touch: paths, hosts, commands. Enforced before the tool runs. Permission: a tool_call outside the allowed paths is refused before it runs agents.md

items.name: gate
items.text: User approval required before a tool runs. Default for destructive. Gate: the harness asks the user before a destructive tool runs agents.md

items.name: sandbox
items.text: The boundary that contains a tool's effects: files, network, processes. Sandbox: files, network and processes inside the boundary, the machine outside it agents.md

items.name: grounding
items.text: Workspace state the harness injects into context each turn. Grounding: the state of the workspace, injected into the context each turn agents.md

items.name: max_rounds
items.text: Hard cap on rounds per turn. Max rounds: the seventh round never runs agents.md

items.name: budget
items.text: Token, time or cost cap, scoped to a turn, run or session. Budget: token, time and cost bars, scoped to a turn, run or session agents.md

items.name: truncate
items.text: Cut one tool_result to fit. The full output stays in the sidecar. Truncate: one result cut to fit, the whole of it in the sidecar agents.md

items.name: compact
items.text: Replace the older part of the transcript in context with a summary. The replaced messages stay in the transcript and in the sidecar. Compact: older messages replaced by a summary in the context, kept in the transcript agents.md

items.name: stall
items.text: Rounds continue without progress. Reading counts as progress; repeating the same call does not. Stall: the same call five times, nothing moves agents.md

items.name: runaway
items.text: A turn stopped by max_rounds or budget. Runaway: a turn stopped by the cap, not by a final agents.md

items.name: check
items.text: Harness runs tests or lint after final and re-prompts on failure. Extends the turn. The harness runs the tests or the linter after a final and, on a failure, sends it back to the model. It extends the turn: the turn ends at the last final, once the checks pass (MP-60). Check: tests run after the final; a failure goes back as another round agents.md

items.name: review
items.text: One extra call asking a model to inspect the result against the task. Same model, another agent, or a human. Review: one extra call reads the task and the result and gives a verdict agents.md

items.name: handoff
items.text: Agent stops and passes the task and its context to the user or to another agent. Handoff: the task and its context passed whole to the user or another agent agents.md

items.name: design agent
items.text: workspace = canvas or artifact; tools = inspect, render, place, style. Design agent: workspace a canvas, tools inspect, render, place, style agents.md

items.name: embedded agent
items.text: workspace = app data via the app's API; scope enforced by the app's access controls. Embedded agent: workspace app data through its API agents.md

items.name: Happy Path
items.text: the ideal scenario without errors Happy path: the green road of steps, the grey error branches never taken testing.md

items.name: Smoke Tests
items.text: a small set of basic tests that verify whether the most critical parts of a system work at all. They answer one question: Does the application run without immediately breaking? If smoke tests fail, deeper testing is usually pointless. (Why "smoke"? From hardware: Power it on – if smoke comes out, something is seriously broken.) Smoke tests: power on, does it run at all; the deep tests wait behind testing.md

items.name: Edge Case
items.text: a situation at an extreme of the input – an empty list, the first or the last item, the maximum size – where code written for the usual case breaks Edge case: the usual range in green, the empty, first, last and maximum in red testing.md

items.name: Transient Error
items.text: temporary issues that resolve quickly Transient error: two failed tries, a wait, the third answered testing.md

items.name: Intermittent Failure
items.text: a failure that happens sometimes, unpredictably A failure of the application that happens sometimes, unpredictably, and usually cannot be reproduced consistently. Request 1 works, request 2 fails, request 3 works again — even though nothing was changed. A test that fails this way is a flaky test. Common causes: timing issues and race conditions, network instability, concurrency issues (threads or processes interfering), uninitialized values, hardware flakiness (bad RAM, overheating), resource limits hit sometimes (a connection pool exhausted). Painful because it does not fail every time, logs often do not show a clear cause, and "works on my machine" happens a lot. Intermittent failure: six requests to the same code, two of them failing, nothing changed testing.md

items.name: Error Flood
items.text: scenario with 75% errors (?) Provisional: not defined yet. The author's note reads "a scenario with 75% errors", a working name kept until the author settles what it means (MP-62). Error flood: forty requests, thirty of them failed testing.md

items.name: Flaky Test
items.text: tests that produce inconsistent results, sometimes passing and sometimes failing, without any changes to the code or test being tested A test that passes and fails by turns with no change to the code or to the test. The fault is in the test (a fixed timeout, an order it relies on) or an intermittent failure under it. Flaky test: one unchanged test, red and green by turns through the week testing.md

items.name: Showstopper Bug
items.text: a defect so severe that it prevents the system from functioning or blocks further progress (development, testing, or release). Work cannot reasonably continue until it is fixed. Showstopper bug: the road from development to customers blocked by a barrier testing.md

items.name: Self-check
items.text: the application's own check that it is fit to work, as a car checks itself on the dashboard: one lamp per thing it needs, the programs it calls, the variables, the folders, what its build produced, each dark when the thing is there and works, lit when it is not. It reads and reports, changes nothing; one lit lamp names what to fix and stops it The application checks, by itself, that it is fit to work, as a car checks itself on the dashboard: one lamp per thing it needs, dark when that thing is there and works, lit when it is not. The lamps are the programs it calls, the environment variables, the folders it writes, the port, the versions, and what its own build was to produce. A lit lamp is the whole answer: the application is not fit, and the lamp names what to fix. It changes nothing: a self-check reads and reports. When every lamp is dark it says one line or nothing; when one is lit it names it and stops, before any work is half done. It runs where there is something new to check: the last step of the build (PROJ-30), so an image that fails it is never shipped; and again as the first step of the run when the host may differ from the build, so a host that fails it does no work. One probe per lamp, each in its own strict shell, its output prefixed with the lamp's name, so the log says which one lit. Present is not enough: a probe exercises the tool the way the application will use it (a font subset must come out smaller with zopfli; a time zone the data uses must be known to the runtime), for the usual failure is a tool that is there and misconfigured. Beside its neighbours: bin/configure makes the environment, the self-check tells whether it is as made (PROJ-02). A smoke test asks the same question from outside, by a test run now and then; the self-check is asked by the application itself, on every build or start. A health check is the probe of a running service, asked again and again; the self-check runs once. Self-check, not self-test: a test is run against the code, by bin/test ; a check is what the application does to itself and its surroundings, as a driver reads the dashboard before setting out. The command is bin/self-check , named for who checks: the application, not a tester from outside. A script named for one lamp, check-env for the environment, is one lamp of it; the self-check is the whole dashboard, and the build's last step adds the lamps of its own output, the folders it was to produce. Self-check: a dashboard of lamps, one lit, naming the port to fix testing.md

items.name: Safety net
items.text: a second, independent catch under the first way: when the usual mechanism fails or is forgotten, the net limits the damage. Not the plan, but what holds when the plan does not The net under the trapeze: the act is done without it, and nobody falls on purpose, but when someone does, the net is what holds. In software, a second mechanism, independent of the first, that catches what the first lets through and limits the damage: a timeout behind a request that should return, a cap on a loop that should end, a job that puts back what a step should have put back. It is not the way things are meant to work; it is what holds when they do not. An example: an agent is switched to the strongest model for one message, and the reply is meant to switch it back. The safety net: if the agent is still on the strongest model ten minutes after that message's reply, the app switches it back itself and says so in the log. The switch-back after the reply is the plan; the ten-minute check is the net. Beside its neighbours: a self-check asks before the work whether the application is fit; an integrity check asks after it whether the data is still whole; a safety net sits under the work itself and acts when the first mechanism did not. A fallback is a second way to the same result; a safety net does not finish the job, it stops a miss from spreading. A good net is simple and independent, so it cannot fail for the same reason as what it guards, and it says when it caught something: every catch is a sign that the first way failed, and worth a look. Safety net: the plan as a rope across, the miss falling into the net below testing.md

items.name: vocabulary
items.text: which words we have/use Vocabulary: our words as pills, the words we do not use struck through README.md

items.name: glossary
items.text: the words of a vocabulary, with their description and meaning Glossary: a table of terms, each with its meaning README.md

items.name: dictionary
items.text: every word of a language, in order, each with all its meanings Every word of a language, or of a whole field, in alphabetical order, each with all its meanings, its part of speech and how it is used. Where a glossary keeps only our words and the one meaning we give each, a dictionary keeps every word and every meaning; a glossary is chosen, a dictionary is complete. In code a dictionary is something else: a map from keys to values ( user_by_id ). Dictionary: process, provider and proxy under P, process with two numbered meanings README.md

items.name: tree
items.text: One root; every other node has exactly one parent; no circles. Folders, outlines, an org chart. One root, and every other node has exactly one parent, so there are no circles and exactly one path from the root to any node. Folders, an outline, an org chart, a family line. In the agent notes: the folders of a note (agentdir, commondir, messages, roadmaps). A thread is a tree as long as each message answers one message. A tree is a graph with rules; a taxonomy is a tree of kinds. Tree: the folders of a note maps.md

items.name: graph
items.text: Nodes and edges, directed or not, with no rule on how they link: several parents, circles. Things (nodes) and the links between them (edges), directed or not, with no rule on how they link: a node may have several parents, and links may run in circles. The pages of this site are a graph: the README links to Rules and to Glossaries, Rules links to Glossaries, Glossaries to Agents, and Agents back to Rules. Glossaries has two parents, and three pages link in a circle; a tree allows neither. Trees, taxonomies and ontologies are all graphs with rules added. Graph: the pages of this site and the links between them, one page with two parents and three pages in a circle maps.md

items.name: map
items.text: A smaller picture that keeps what matters of something bigger and leaves the rest out on purpose. A smaller picture that keeps what matters of something bigger: where things are and how they connect. "The map is not the territory": a map leaves things out on purpose. In code, a map (a dictionary) goes from keys to values, one value per key. Also a mind map, a concept map, a site map. In the agent notes: a roadmap is a map of the way; "the terms and how they relate" below is a concept map; a glossary maps each term to its meaning. Map maps.md

items.name: taxonomy
items.text: Kinds and kinds of kinds, each one "is a" the one above it (animal › bird › owl). A tree of kinds. Sorting into kinds and kinds of kinds, each one "is a" the one above it: animal › bird › owl. Linnaeus for living things, the shelves of a library. In the agent notes: a message is the author's or the agent's; a page is a subject file, a cover or a plan; a marker is .working or .cancelled . A taxonomy is a tree, and the backbone of an ontology, which adds the other links. Taxonomy: the kinds of things in a note maps.md

items.name: ontology
items.text: The concepts of a field, their instances, the relations between them and their rules, written down. In philosophy, the study of what exists. In computing, a written map of what a field talks about, in four parts: the kinds of things (a message, a conversation, a subject file), the things themselves (your message of this morning asking for a glossary is a message), the relations between them (a conversation is made of messages; a reply answers a message) and the rules (every conversation has exactly one subject file). It is written down so that people and programs use the words the same way: RDF and OWL are the standards, Schema.org the best known on the web. A glossary defines words one by one; an ontology also says how they connect. Written down once, a rename (workdir became subjectdir) happens in one place, and an agent can check a word against it. Ontology: the words of a note and how they connect The terms of this glossary and how they relate maps.md

items.name: knowledge graph
items.text: An ontology filled with real things: not "a message answers a message" but "this reply answers that message". An ontology filled with real things: not "a reply answers a message" in general, but "my reply of 09:30 answers your message of 09:17", one link for each pair that has it. What search engines and AI retrieval use. In the agent notes: every message, subject file and plan of a note with their links; the app could build it, and it would feed an agent's context. Knowledge graph: the ontology on the left, this note's real messages and links on the right maps.md

items.name: roadmap
items.text: The whole way ahead: where we go and in what order, not exactly when. Now / Next / Later. The whole way ahead: where we are going and in what order, not exactly when. A product roadmap is often three columns, Now / Next / Later. It changes as we learn, and it is meant to be shown, so it stays coarse: themes and stages, not tasks. In the agent notes: an agent's plan for one conversation, roadmaps/<time -agent-plan.md , its parts - [ ] P1 … ticked as each is done, new ones added at the end; and the author's roadmaps in the app, lists of work across projects. A roadmap is laid on a timeline, marked by milestones and fed by a backlog. Roadmap maps.md

items.name: milestone
items.text: One point on the way, reached or not. Takes no time, unlike a task. The Roman stone by the road that said how far it was to Rome. In a project, a point that is reached or not ("Released", "Signed"); it takes no time, unlike a task. A diamond on a Gantt chart; on GitHub, a group of issues with a due date. In the agent notes: the goal's steps in a subject file, drawn under the cover: done, now or next. The step that is now waits on the agent while it works and on the author after its reply; a step is named as it stands ("Testing" while now, "Tested" once done); the last is always "Done: nothing left, to the archive". Milestone maps.md

items.name: breadcrumbs
items.text: The trail behind: from the root to where you stand, each crumb a way back (Home › Docs › Page). The trail that shows where you are and how you got there, as in Hansel and Gretel; on a web page, Home › Docs › Page, each crumb a link back up. Against roadmap and milestone: breadcrumbs look back (the way behind, from the root to here), a roadmap looks ahead (the whole way, in order), and a milestone is one stone on that way. A milestone passed is, in effect, a breadcrumb. In the agent notes: the path agentdir › commondir › Terms , and the chain of Re: lines back to a conversation's first message. Breadcrumbs, roadmap and milestone side by side maps.md

items.name: timeline
items.text: Events placed along time. Events placed along time. In the agent notes: the change log at the end of each subject file, and the times in message names. A roadmap is laid on one. Timeline: the events of this morning along one line maps.md

items.name: chronology
items.text: Events in the order they happened, each with its time; the gaps between them not drawn. Events in the order they happened, each with its date or time, at even steps: the order and the times count, not the distance between them. It fits what a user did over time: first one thing, then another, then a third. A long gap is cut short, its length written on the cut. In the agent notes: a conversation's messages, first to last, each with its time in its name. A timeline puts each event at its moment, so the gaps show; in a chronology a night between two visits takes no more room than a minute. Chronology: one user's seven actions evenly along a line, from opening the pricing page to upgrading the next day, the 23-hour night cut short maps.md

items.name: backlog
items.text: Work known but not yet planned, in no fixed order. The work known but not yet planned, in no fixed order. In the agent notes: the "what is next" list of a subject file, the parts not yet on a roadmap. It feeds a roadmap. Backlog: a pile of cards in no order, and the three columns of the roadmap they feed maps.md

items.name: anatomy
items.text: The parts of one thing seen whole, each named where it sits (a button: container, icon, label). The parts of one thing, seen whole: each part named where it sits, in the thing it belongs to. Borrowed from biology (the anatomy of a hand), it is common in computing: the anatomy of a button (a container, an icon on the left, a label beside it), of a URL (scheme, host, path, query, in that order), of a log line or of a file. Design systems give each component page an Anatomy section: the component drawn once, each part numbered in place, the names beside. In the agent notes: a message as the app shows it, its header on top, its text, a voice comment's player with the transcript under it, a screenshot last. A taxonomy sorts many things into kinds ("is a"); an anatomy opens one thing ("part of"). The parts taken out and set in a tree are a meronomy, which keeps what holds what but loses where each part sits: the anatomy is the picture of the whole, usually a labelled diagram. Anatomy: one message seen whole, its five parts numbered where they sit maps.md

items.name: labelled diagram
items.text: A thing drawn whole, a thin line from each part to its name. A thing drawn whole, as it is seen, with a thin line (a callout, or leader line) from each part to its name. Nothing is moved and nothing is opened, so only the outside can be named. The common picture of an anatomy: a diagram of a flower in a school book, a device's parts in its manual, a component in a design system. What is inside stays hidden; a cutaway opens it, an exploded view takes it apart. Labelled diagram: a hand coffee grinder whole, a line from each part to its name maps.md

items.name: exploded view
items.text: A thing's parts pulled apart along the lines they fit on, numbered for a parts list. The parts of a thing pulled apart along the lines they fit on, each in the place it goes, so that every part is seen and the order of putting them together can be read off the picture. Each part has a number; the numbers lead to a parts list (in industry, a bill of materials). An assembly sheet of flat-pack furniture is one. It shows what a labelled diagram cannot: the parts behind other parts, and how they go together. Exploded view: the same grinder, its seven parts pulled apart along their axis and numbered, with the parts list maps.md

items.name: cutaway
items.text: A thing drawn with part of its casing taken away, so the inside shows. A thing drawn whole with part of its casing taken away, so the inside shows in its place: the gears of a clock behind its face, the rooms of a ship behind its hull. The edge of the cut is drawn, so it reads as opened, not as missing. Unlike an exploded view nothing moves: the inside is seen where it works. Only what the cut opens is named; the outside is the labelled diagram's. Cutaway: the same grinder with its front cut open, the shaft, the burrs and the ground coffee named maps.md

items.name: legend
items.text: The key of a picture: what each colour, line and sign means, set apart from the drawing. The key of a picture: a small box, set apart from the drawing, with a sample of each colour, line and sign and what it means. A map's legend says that a blue line is a river and a dashed red one a border; a chart's says which colour is which series. In British English also a key. A label names one thing on the drawing itself; a caption says under the picture what the whole shows; a legend explains the marks, once, for all of them. In the agent notes: the overview's colours (green done, orange waits on the author, the accent at work), and the two samples at the top of this page's terms map. Legend: a small map of roads, a river, a border and a park, its legend beside it maps.md

items.name: morphing
items.text: One element turns into another: its shape, size and place change through every frame between, so the eye follows it as one. One element turns into another: its shape, size and place change through every frame between, so the eye follows it as the same thing, never one thing swapped for another. A menu grows out of its button and shrinks back into it; a chip opens into its field; a card's avatar shrinks into its folded line while the time moves beside it. It is the ideal animation: almost every animation rule is built on it. What comes from something on the screen, or goes into it, morphs (ANIM-16); only what has nothing to come from fades. Morphing: the menu grows out of its button and back, the toast only fades motion.md

items.name: fade
items.text: An element comes or goes by its opacity alone, where it stands: the simplest smooth change. An element comes or goes by its opacity alone, where it stands, its shape and place unchanged: the simplest smooth change. It is for what has nothing to morph from or into, a toast or a tooltip, and for the parts of a morph that have no place in the other shape (ANIM-10). Never whole on one frame and gone on the next. Fade: the toast comes and goes by its opacity, where it stands motion.md

items.name: system
items.text: The whole: every part working together for one purpose. Also: platform, stack, infrastructure, application, setup, ecosystem. The whole: every part working together for one purpose, the browser, the services, the databases and the providers outside. A word for when the parts matter less than what they do together. Also: platform (others build on it), stack (layers on top of each other), infrastructure (what runs the rest), application (what the user touches), setup (one arrangement of it), ecosystem (many owners). On the Agents glossary system is the system message, not this. System: a browser, two services, a database and an outside provider in one frame, working for one purpose architecture.md

items.name: service
items.text: A program that keeps running and answers requests from others. Also: server, daemon, backend, endpoint, API, microservice. A program that keeps running and answers requests from others, often over the network: started once, then waiting, serving many callers in turn. Also: server (the program or the machine it runs on), daemon (runs in the background, no screen), backend (behind a front end), endpoint or API (its doorway, not the whole), microservice (one small service among many). "A service" may also mean what is offered, not the program: then facility or utility . Service: three callers send requests to one running service and each gets its answer architecture.md

items.name: provider
items.text: What supplies something the rest needs, one of several that could. Also: source, supplier, vendor, backend, adapter, driver. What supplies something the rest needs (files, sign-in, e-mail, payments), one of several that could: the code asks for the thing, and whichever provider is plugged in gives it. Also: source (where data comes from), supplier , vendor (a company), backend (the one behind a common front), adapter or driver (one swappable piece of code per provider). Provider: the app asks for storage; the disk provider is plugged in, the cloud and memory providers could take its place architecture.md

items.name: module
items.text: One part of the code with a job of its own, used by the rest only through what it exports. Also: component, unit, package, library, plugin. One part of the code with a job of its own, used by the rest only through what it exports. Inside it may change freely; its exports are its promise. Also: component (a part, often of a screen), unit (the smallest part tested alone), package or library (shipped and versioned apart), plugin or extension (added from outside), building block . Module: three modules in one codebase; each is used only through its exports, its inside hidden architecture.md

items.name: process
items.text: A running program, its own memory, from start to exit. Also: worker, instance. A running program: its own memory, its own id (pid), from start to exit. The operating system runs it; it runs jobs, tasks and functions. A worker is a process that takes jobs from a queue; an instance is one of several copies of the same program. "Process" may also mean a way of doing things, not a program: then procedure or workflow . Process: one running program with its pid and memory, started, running its jobs, then exiting architecture.md

items.name: job
items.text: Work handed over to run later or apart, with an id and a status. Also: batch, run. Work handed over to run later or apart: it gets an id and a status the caller can look up, queued, running, done or failed, and may be retried or run on a schedule. Also: batch (many items in one job), run (one execution of it). Tools draw the lines their own way: in CI a job holds steps, in Kubernetes a Job starts pods. Job: queued, running, then done or failed; a failed job is retried architecture.md

items.name: task
items.text: One unit of work, one step of a job. Also: step, operation, work item. One unit of work to do: one step of a job, small enough to finish or fail as a whole. Often a function call put in a queue. Also: step (one in an order), operation , work item . Task: a job of three tasks, resize, save and upload, done one after another architecture.md

items.name: function
items.text: Code with a name: called with arguments, it returns. Also: routine, subroutine, procedure, method. Code with a name: called with arguments, it returns a value. No life of its own; it runs for the length of one call. Also: routine or subroutine , procedure (often one that returns nothing), method (a function of an object). Function: resize is called with an image and a width and returns the smaller image architecture.md

items.name: pipeline
items.text: Stages in a row, the output of each the input of the next. Also: workflow, flow, stream, assembly line. Stages in a row, the output of each the input of the next: data goes in at one end and comes out changed at the other. Each stage does one thing and knows only its neighbours, so all of them can be busy at once, each with its own item. A shell's a b c , a build, a CI pipeline. Also: workflow (the steps, often with people in them), flow , stream (items one by one, without end), assembly line . Pipeline: photos go through resize, compress and upload and come out as thumbnails, each stage busy with its own photo architecture.md

items.name: chain
items.text: Links one after another, each handing on to the next or stopping there. Also: sequence, series, cascade. Links one after another, each handing on to the next or stopping there. What goes along is control, a request or a call, not data being changed: middleware ( next() ), a promise chain ( .then() ), method chaining, a chain of responsibility. Where a pipeline changes data stage by stage, a chain passes a turn, and any link may end it. Also: sequence , series , cascade (each step sets off the next). Chain: a request passes log and auth to the handler; auth may stop it with a 401 architecture.md
